Matching algebras and their Dunkl subalgebras

Darij Grinberg Address: Department of Mathematics, Drexel University, Philadelphia, PA, USA Email address: darijgrinberg@gmail.com , Anatol Kirillov Address: Yanqi Lake Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Huairou District, Beijing, China Email address: kirillov@bimsa.cn and Boris Shapiro Address: Department of Mathematics, Stockholm University, Stockholm, Sweden Email address: shapiro@math.su.se
Date: 2 October 2026
Abstract.

For a finite simple graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), we consider the quotient algebra ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) of the polynomial ring in the variables ueu_{e} (for e∈Ee\in E) by the ideal generated by all products ue​ufu_{e}u_{f} for non-disjoint edges ee and ff (this includes all squares ue2u_{e}^{2}). This quotient is called the matching algebra of GG, since it has a basis indexed by the matchings of GG. In this quotient, we define a subalgebra 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) generated by the signed incidence sums θv=∑e=(v,w)ue−∑e=(w,v)ue\theta_{v}=\sum_{e=(v,w)}u_{e}-\sum_{e=(w,v)}u_{e} for all v∈Vv\in V (where all edges of GG are oriented arbitrarily); we call this the Dunkl matching algebra.

We show that, as a graded vector space, 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) is dual to the span of all polynomials pM=∏(i,j)∈M(xi−xj)p_{M}=\prod_{(i,j)\in M}(x_{i}-x_{j}), where MM ranges over all matchings of GG. For the complete graph KnK_{n}, the latter span is a direct sum of two-row Specht modules (one in each degree); thus its Hilbert series is that of the Catalan triangle, and, in characteristic zero, the Dunkl matching algebra can be presented by linear and quadratic relations. For arbitrary graphs, we formulate the saturation problem of deciding when the selected matching Specht generators pMp_{M} in a given degree kk span the full two-row Specht module S(n−k,k)S^{(n-k,k)}. We show that saturation in degree kk forces kk-connectivity, that saturation in degree 22 is equivalent to 22-connectivity, and that kk-linked graphs are saturated in degree kk. We also prove saturation in every possible degree whenever the complement of GG is a matching. We show that the Dunkl matching algebra equals the full matching algebra exactly for forests, and give an explicit Hilbert series formula for unicyclic graphs. Finally, we compare with a related Postnikov–Shapiro quotient: depending on the ambient algebra, its Hilbert series is either the central zonotopal specialization of the Tutte polynomial or a regraded all-terminal reliability polynomial.

Key words and phrases: 
matching, Dunkl element, Specht polynomial, graph connectivity, Specht module, Lefschetz property, zonotopal algebra, Tutte polynomial

Primary 05E10, 05C70; Secondary 13A02, 05B35

1. Introduction

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite simple graph. The matching generating polynomial of GG records the numbers of sets of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges. In this note we lift this elementary invariant to a graded algebra

ℳ(G)=𝐤[ue:e∈E]/(ueuf:e∩f≠∅).\mathcal{M}(G)=\mathbf{k}[u_{e}:e\in E]/(u_{e}u_{f}:e\cap f\neq\varnothing).

In this algebra, we define the signed incidence sums

θv=∑e=(v,w)ue−∑e=(w,v)ue for all ​v∈V,\theta_{v}=\sum_{e=(v,w)}u_{e}-\sum_{e=(w,v)}u_{e}\qquad\text{ for all }v\in V,

where an orientation of GG has been chosen. We denote by 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) the subalgebra generated by the θv\theta_{v} and call it the Dunkl matching algebra. The goal of the present note is to understand this algebra 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G), in particular its Hilbert series.

The homogeneous parts 𝒟​(G)k\mathcal{D}(G)_{k} of 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) stand in a natural duality to certain subspaces of the polynomial ring 𝐤⁡[xv∣v∈V]\mathbf{k}[x_{v}\mid v\in V]. Namely, for each matching MM, define the polynomial

pM=pM​(x)=∏(i,j)∈M(xi−xj)∈𝐤⁡[xv∣v∈V].p_{M}=p_{M}(x)=\prod_{(i,j)\in M}(x_{i}-x_{j})\in\mathbf{k}[x_{v}\mid v\in V].

For any k≥0k\geq 0, we define the vector subspace

Pk​(G):=span𝐤⁡{pM:M​ is a k-matching of G} of ​𝐤​[xv∣v∈V].P_{k}(G):=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf{k}}\{p_{M}:M\text{ is a $k$-matching of $G$}\}\qquad\text{ of }\mathbf{k}[x_{v}\mid v\in V].

The main results we shall show are the following:

  • •

    For each k≥0k\geq 0, we have

    dim𝒟​(G)k=dimPk​(G);\dim\mathcal{D}(G)_{k}=\dim P_{k}(G);

    see Theorem 3.2. More precisely, the proof gives a canonical perfect pairing between 𝒟​(G)k\mathcal{D}(G)_{k} and Pk​(G)P_{k}(G) (see Remark 3.3); thus, Pk​(G)P_{k}(G) becomes a dual polynomial model for 𝒟​(G)k\mathcal{D}(G)_{k}. Consequently, the Hilbert function of 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) records the ranks of the matching-restricted products ∏(i,j)∈M(xi−xj)\prod_{(i,j)\in M}(x_{i}-x_{j}).

  • •

    For the complete graph KnK_{n}, the dual polynomial model becomes classical representation theory: for 0≤k≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor,

    Pk​(Kn)≅S(n−k,k).P_{k}(K_{n})\cong S^{(n-k,k)}.

    Here S(n−k,k)S^{(n-k,k)} is the Specht module of shape (n−k,k)(n-k,k) (and is irreducible in characteristic zero). Thus, the Hilbert series of 𝒟⁡(Kn)\mathcal{D}(K_{n}) is the generating function of the nn-th row of the Catalan triangle; see Theorem 4.1. In characteristic zero, we also obtain the presentation

    𝒟⁡(Kn)≅𝐤⁡[z1,…,zn]/(z1+⋯+zn,z12,…,zn2);\mathcal{D}(K_{n})\cong\mathbf{k}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}]/(z_{1}+\cdots+z_{n},z_{1}^{2},\ldots,z_{n}^{2});

    see Theorem 4.4.

  • •

    Motivated by the complete-graph case, we say that a graph GG is kk-saturated when Pk​(G)=Pk​(Kn)P_{k}(G)=P_{k}(K_{n}). We prove the implications

    k​-linked⟹k​-saturated⟹k​-connected;k\text{-linked}\ \Longrightarrow\ k\text{-saturated}\ \Longrightarrow\ k\text{-connected};

    see Propositions 5.11 and 5.4. In degree 22 the second implication is an equivalence:

    P2(G)=P2(Kn)⟺G is 2-connectedP_{2}(G)=P_{2}(K_{n})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G\text{ is $2$-connected}

    for n≥4n\geq 4; see Theorem 5.9. We also show that if G¯\overline{G} is a matching, then GG is saturated in every possible degree; see Theorem 5.12.

  • •

    The matching generating polynomial and the Dunkl Hilbert series of GG (that is, the Hilbert series of 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G)) are incomparable invariants: neither determines the other. Indeed, P3P_{3} and K3K_{3} have the same Dunkl Hilbert series 1+2​t1+2t but different matching generating polynomials 1+2​t1+2t and 1+3​t1+3t, respectively; in the other direction, Proposition 5.17 gives graphs with the same matching generating polynomial but different Dunkl Hilbert series. We also obtain explicit positive formulas in sparse cases. Namely,

    𝒟(G)=ℳ(G)⟺G is a forest;\mathcal{D}(G)=\mathcal{M}(G)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G\text{ is a forest};

    see Proposition 5.15. For a unicyclic graph with unique cycle CC and F=G−V⁡(C)F=G-V(C), we obtain a short exact sequence of graded vector spaces

    0⟶ℳ⁡(F)​(−1)⟶ℳ⁡(G)⟶⨁k≥0Pk​(G)⟶0,0\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}(F)(-1)\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}(G)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}P_{k}(G)\longrightarrow 0,

    and hence (using the notation 𝔪G\mathfrak{m}_{G} for the matching generating polynomial of GG)

    Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)=𝔪G​(t)−t​𝔪F​(t);\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)=\mathfrak{m}_{G}(t)-t\mathfrak{m}_{F}(t);

    see Theorem 5.16. Minimal pairs with the same matching generating polynomial but different Dunkl Hilbert series occur on 44 vertices in general, on 55 vertices among connected graphs, and on 66 vertices among 22-connected graphs; see Propositions 5.17 and 5.18.

  • •

    Finally, we survey a related construction in the larger square-zero edge algebra [24], where distinct incident edge generators are allowed to multiply. For each nontrivial vertex cut δ⁡(S)\delta(S), consider the cut monomial

    ηS:=∏e∈δ⁡(S)ue,\eta_{S}:=\prod_{e\in\delta(S)}u_{e},

    and impose the relations ηS=0\eta_{S}=0 for all such SS. If these relations are imposed inside the subalgebra generated by the signed incidence sums, the resulting quotient is the central graphical zonotopal algebra. If they are imposed instead in the whole square-zero edge algebra, the surviving monomials are precisely the uFu_{F} for which deleting FF leaves GG connected; hence the Hilbert series counts connected spanning subgraphs and is a specialization of the all-terminal reliability polynomial. See Propositions A.1 and A.2; these results are not new, so we provide no proofs.

Motivation. This work is inspired by the Fomin–Kirillov approach to Schubert calculus, see [10, 2, 18]. However in our set-up the adjective “Dunkl” is motivational only. Unlike the Fomin–Kirillov algebra [10], our matching algebra is commutative and kills every product of two incident edge generators.

Recall that the Fomin–Kirillov quadratic algebra ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n} is generated by antisymmetric symbols [i​j]=−[j​i][ij]=-[ji] subject, in particular, to [i​j]2=0[ij]^{2}=0, commutation of generators with disjoint supports, and certain three-term relations on triples of indices. Its distinguished elements

ϑi=∑j≠i[i​j]\vartheta_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}[ij]

are known as the Dunkl elements. A fundamental feature of the construction is that these elements commute, and the commutative subalgebra which they generate provides an algebraic model for the cohomology ring of the complete flag variety; see [10]. This point of view has subsequently led to variants for other Coxeter groups, quantum cohomology, KK-theory, and Nichols–Woronowicz algebras.

Blasiak, Liu, and Mészáros [7, Definition 2.3] have introduced restrictions of this algebra to a graph. For a graph GG on [n][n], they define ℰG\mathcal{E}_{G} to be the subalgebra of ℰn\mathcal{E}_{n} generated by those [i​j][ij] for which {i,j}\{i,j\} is an edge of GG. Their graph restriction is thus a subalgebra construction, rather than the quotient obtained by setting nonedge generators equal to zero.

Our construction may be viewed as a quotient of this picture. Give the generator corresponding to an unoriented edge {i,j}\{i,j\} the sign determined by an orientation and write it as ui​j=−uj​iu_{ij}=-u_{ji}. If, in addition to the Fomin–Kirillov relations, one kills every product

ui​j​uk​ℓwith{i,j}∩{k,ℓ}≠∅,u_{ij}u_{k\ell}\qquad\text{with}\qquad\{i,j\}\cap\{k,\ell\}\neq\varnothing,

and kills the generators corresponding to nonedges of GG, then the resulting commutative quotient is precisely the matching algebra ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G). Under this quotient the Dunkl element ϑi\vartheta_{i} descends to the signed incidence sum θi\theta_{i}. Thus 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) can be interpreted as the part of the Dunkl-element construction which survives after only products supported on matchings are retained. Equivalently, the quotient map ℰn↠ℳ⁡(Kn)\mathcal{E}_{n}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{M}(K_{n}) that kills products of incident edge generators restricts to a surjection ℰG↠ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{E}_{G}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{M}(G), where ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) is identified with the subalgebra of ℳ⁡(Kn)\mathcal{M}(K_{n}) generated by the edges of GG.

This truncation changes the nature of the problem considerably. The flag-variety and Bruhat-order connections of the classical setting are replaced by the incidence structure of a graph, while the linear forms xi−xjx_{i}-x_{j}, i.e., the roots of type AA, reappear on the dual side. One may therefore ask how much of the structure carried by Dunkl elements survives under this severe matching truncation. The results below show that the answer retains a surprising amount of structure: for the complete graph the homogeneous components are governed by two-row Specht modules, whereas for arbitrary graphs the failure or success of spanning the corresponding Specht module detects connectivity properties of the graph. In this sense, the matching quotient provides a bridge between the Dunkl-element philosophy, matching theory, and the representation theory of the symmetric group.

Related work. Subalgebras generated by vertices in the commutative algebra generated by edges have been considered in e.g., [24, 25]. Moreover, in the case of complete graphs they also have a geometric interpretation, see [26]. Products of arbitrary subfamilies of a vector configuration have a rich theory related to Tutte polynomials; see Berget [5] and the zonotopal literature [1, 15]. Our restriction to vertex-disjoint subfamilies is not matroidal: it remembers the incidence of edges at vertices. It also differs from graph Specht modules and their relationship with matching polytopes studied by Liu [21]. The construction lies naturally between these two subjects.

Several nearby constructions attach graded objects to matchings but use a different algebraic mechanism. Numata [23] studies an Artinian Gorenstein algebra obtained by apolarity from a weighted matching generating function and proves a strong Lefschetz property. Li [19] proves strong equivariant log-concavity for the graded permutation representation on the matchings of an arbitrary graph. For perfect matchings of complete graphs, Filmus and Lindzey [11] develop harmonic polynomial models involving Specht polynomials and matching-inclusion matrices. Bedratyuk’s graph algebra [4], whose basis is indexed by all simple graphs on a fixed vertex set, also carries Boolean up/down operators and two-row Specht modules. Bergeron, Chan, Soltani, and Zabrocki [3] study a construction deceptively parallel to our Pk​(Kn)P_{k}(K_{n}) in an exterior algebra: products of differences ξj−ξi\xi_{j}-\xi_{i} indexed by noncrossing pairings give bases of exterior quasisymmetric harmonic spaces whose degree-kk dimensions agree with dimPk​(Kn)\dim P_{k}(K_{n}). We compare the two constructions more closely in Remark 4.3. None of these constructions is the incidence-generated subalgebra 𝒟⁡(G)⊆ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G)\subseteq\mathcal{M}(G) studied here.

There is one direct overlap at the level of the abstract complete-graph presentation. Jonsson Kling, Lundqvist, Mohammadi, Orth, and Sáenz-de-Cabezón [17] study the more general almost complete intersections

𝐤⁡[z1,…,zn]/(z12,…,zn2,(z1+⋯+zn)q).\mathbf{k}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}]/(z_{1}^{2},\ldots,z_{n}^{2},(z_{1}+\cdots+z_{n})^{q}).

The quotient occurring in our characteristic-zero presentation of 𝒟⁡(Kn)\mathcal{D}(K_{n}) is their case q=1q=1. The contribution here is therefore not the abstract quotient itself, but its realization inside a matching algebra, its matching-product duality, and the resulting saturation problem for arbitrary graphs.

Notations. Throughout, 𝐤\mathbf{k} is a field. In some places, we will additionally assume that 𝐤\mathbf{k} has characteristic zero.

2. The matching algebra

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite simple graph. Its edges are 22-element sets of vertices; thus, two edges e,fe,f satisfy e∩f≠∅e\cap f\neq\varnothing if and only if they have a common endpoint (this allows e=fe=f). Two edges ee and ff are said to be incident if e∩f≠∅e\cap f\neq\varnothing.

Definition 2.1.

The matching algebra of GG is the commutative 𝐤\mathbf{k}-algebra

ℳ(G):=𝐤[ue:e∈E]/(ueuf:e∩f≠∅).\mathcal{M}(G):=\mathbf{k}[u_{e}:e\in E]/\bigl(u_{e}u_{f}:e\cap f\neq\varnothing\bigr).

That is, ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) is the quotient of the polynomial ring 𝐤[ue:e∈E]\mathbf{k}[u_{e}:e\in E] by the monomial ideal generated by all products ue​ufu_{e}u_{f} with ee and ff being two incident edges (including the case e=fe=f). It is graded by degree, where every generator ueu_{e} has degree 11.

For a matching M⊆EM\subseteq E of GG, define the element

uM:=∏e∈Mue∈ℳ⁡(G), in particular ​u∅:=1.u_{M}:=\prod_{e\in M}u_{e}\in\mathcal{M}(G),\qquad\text{ in particular }u_{\varnothing}:=1.
Proposition 2.2.

The elements uMu_{M}, indexed by the matchings MM of GG, form a homogeneous 𝐤\mathbf{k}-basis of ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G). Consequently, the Hilbert series of ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) is

Hilb⁡(ℳ⁡(G),t)=∑k≥0mk​(G)​tk,\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{M}(G),t)=\sum_{k\geq 0}m_{k}(G)t^{k},

where mk​(G)m_{k}(G) is the number of kk-matchings of GG.

Proof.

The defining ideal (ueuf:e∩f≠∅)\bigl(u_{e}u_{f}:e\cap f\neq\varnothing\bigr) is monomial. Its standard monomials are the square-free products ue1ue2⋯ueku_{e_{1}}u_{e_{2}}\cdots u_{e_{k}} of generators such that no two of the edges e1,e2,…,eke_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{k} have a common endpoint; these are exactly the uMu_{M} corresponding to the matchings MM of GG. Thus, these uMu_{M} (or, rather, their residue classes) form a basis of the quotient algebra ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G). The formula for the Hilbert series follows directly from this. ∎

Thus, for the complete graph KnK_{n}, we have

Hilb⁡(ℳ⁡(Kn),t)=∑0≤k≤n/2n!2k​k!​(n−2​k)!​tk,\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{M}(K_{n}),t)=\sum_{0\leq k\leq n/2}\frac{n!}{2^{k}k!(n-2k)!}t^{k},

and the complete bipartite graph Ka,bK_{a,b} satisfies

Hilb⁡(ℳ⁡(Ka,b),t)=∑k≥0k!​(ak)​(bk)​tk.\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{M}(K_{a,b}),t)=\sum_{k\geq 0}k!\binom{a}{k}\binom{b}{k}t^{k}.

In particular, dimℳ⁡(Kn)\dim\mathcal{M}(K_{n}) is the number of involutions in SnS_{n}.

Equivalently, if Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) denotes the matching complex of GG (the independence complex of the line graph L⁡(G)L(G)), then ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) is the Artinian monomial quotient obtained from its Stanley–Reisner ring 𝐤⁡[Δ⁡(G)]\mathbf{k}[\Delta(G)] by adjoining the squares ue2u_{e}^{2} to the Stanley–Reisner ideal. Thus ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) itself is not a Stanley–Reisner ring in the usual sense. Matching complexes and their face rings are classical; see, for example, Björner–Lovász–Vrećica–Živaljević [6] and Jonsson [16, Chapter 5]. Ferrarello and Fröberg [9] explicitly relate the Hilbert series of the ordinary Stanley–Reisner ring of a matching complex to graph-subgraph polynomials.

More directly, Dao and Nair [8] associate to an arbitrary simplicial complex Δ\Delta the square-zero face algebra

A⁡(Δ):=𝐤⁡[x1,…,xm]/(IΔ,x12,…,xm2),A(\Delta):=\mathbf{k}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}]/(I_{\Delta},x_{1}^{2},\ldots,x_{m}^{2}),

and study its Lefschetz properties. Thus our matching algebra is exactly ℳ⁡(G)=A⁡(Δ⁡(G))\mathcal{M}(G)=A(\Delta(G)). Such algebras are also a special case of the quadratic monomial quotients studied by Migliore, Nagel, and Schenck [22]. What we shall study (starting in the next section) is a certain subalgebra 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) of ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G), which – to our knowledge – is new.

Example 2.3.

Let G=P4G=P_{4} be the path 1−2−3−41-2-3-4. Then

ℳ⁡(P4)=𝐤⁡[u12,u23,u34]/(u122,u232,u342,u12​u23,u23​u34).\mathcal{M}(P_{4})=\mathbf{k}[u_{12},u_{23},u_{34}]/(u_{12}^{2},u_{23}^{2},u_{34}^{2},u_{12}u_{23},u_{23}u_{34}).

Thus

1,u12,u23,u34,u12​u341,\quad u_{12},\quad u_{23},\quad u_{34},\quad u_{12}u_{34}

is a basis of ℳ⁡(P4)\mathcal{M}(P_{4}). The only nonzero product of two edge generators is u12​u34u_{12}u_{34}, so

Hilb⁡(ℳ⁡(P4),t)=1+3​t+t2,(u12+u34)2=2​u12​u34.\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{M}(P_{4}),t)=1+3t+t^{2},\qquad(u_{12}+u_{34})^{2}=2u_{12}u_{34}.

By contrast, for the triangle K3K_{3} every two edges meet, so ℳ⁡(K3)\mathcal{M}(K_{3}) has basis 1,u12,u13,u231,u_{12},u_{13},u_{23} and its positive-degree ideal has square zero.

3. Signed incidence sums and the Dunkl matching algebra

Fix an orientation of GG. Define incidence coefficients εt,e\varepsilon_{t,e} for all e∈Ee\in E and t∈Vt\in V as follows: If an edge ee is oriented from vv to ww, let

εv,e=1,εw,e=−1,\varepsilon_{v,e}=1,\qquad\varepsilon_{w,e}=-1,

and let all other incidence coefficients εt,e\varepsilon_{t,e} (with t∈V∖{v,w}t\in V\setminus\{v,w\}) be zero.

Definition 3.1.

For v∈Vv\in V, define the signed incidence sum

θv=∑e∈Eεv,e​ue∈ℳ⁡(G).\theta_{v}=\sum_{e\in E}\varepsilon_{v,e}u_{e}\in\mathcal{M}(G).

The Dunkl matching algebra is the graded subalgebra 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) of ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) generated by these signed incidence sums. In other words:

𝒟(G):=𝐤[θv:v∈V]⊆ℳ(G).\mathcal{D}(G):=\mathbf{k}[\theta_{v}:v\in V]\subseteq\mathcal{M}(G).

Reversing the orientation of an edge amounts to replacing the corresponding generator ueu_{e} by −ue-u_{e}; hence the isomorphism type of 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) is orientation-independent. We have

(1) θv2=0,∑v∈Cθv=0\theta_{v}^{2}=0,\qquad\sum_{v\in C}\theta_{v}=0

for every vertex vv and every connected component CC of GG.

Consider the polynomial ring 𝐤⁡[xv∣v∈V]\mathbf{k}[x_{v}\mid v\in V]. If an edge ee is oriented as e=(i,j)e=(i,j), define the linear polynomial pe:=xi−xjp_{e}:=x_{i}-x_{j}. For a matching MM of GG, define the polynomial

(2) pM:=∏e∈Mpe=∏e=(i,j)∈M(xi−xj), so in particular ​p∅:=1.p_{M}:=\prod_{e\in M}p_{e}=\prod_{e=(i,j)\in M}(x_{i}-x_{j}),\qquad\text{ so in particular }p_{\varnothing}:=1.

Reversing the orientation of an edge changes the corresponding pep_{e} and pMp_{M} only by a sign, so all spans considered below are orientation-independent.

For each integer k≥0k\geq 0, we let Matchk⁡(G)\operatorname{Match}_{k}(G) denote the set of all kk-matchings of GG (that is, of all matchings with exactly kk edges), and we define the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-vector subspace

(3) Pk​(G):=span⁡{pM:M∈Matchk⁡(G)}of 𝐤⁡[xv∣v∈V].P_{k}(G):=\operatorname{span}\{p_{M}:M\in\operatorname{Match}_{k}(G)\}\qquad\text{of $\mathbf{k}[x_{v}\mid v\in V]$.}

Consider the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-vector space 𝐤V\mathbf{k}^{V} with basis VV; its standard basis vectors will be denoted by eve_{v}. Let Sk​(𝐤V)S^{k}(\mathbf{k}^{V}) denote its kkth symmetric power. Multiplication gives a linear map

μk:Sk(𝐤V)⟶ℳ(G)k,ev1⋯evk⟼θv1⋯θvk,\mu_{k}:S^{k}(\mathbf{k}^{V})\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}(G)_{k},\qquad e_{v_{1}}\cdots e_{v_{k}}\longmapsto\theta_{v_{1}}\cdots\theta_{v_{k}},

whose image is precisely the kk-th graded component 𝒟​(G)k\mathcal{D}(G)_{k} of 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G).

Theorem 3.2 (Dunkl-polynomial duality).

For every k≥0k\geq 0, we have

Moreover, for α=(αv)v∈V∈ℕV\alpha=(\alpha_{v})_{v\in V}\in\mathbb{N}^{V} with |α|=k|\alpha|=k, write

Orient every displayed edge from the smaller endpoint to the larger one (i.e., orient it as (i,j)(i,j) where i<ji<j).

Proposition 3.5.

The following properties hold.

  1. (1)

    If G=G1⊔G2G=G_{1}\sqcup G_{2}, then 𝒟⁡(G)≅𝒟⁡(G1)⊗𝒟⁡(G2)\mathcal{D}(G)\cong\mathcal{D}(G_{1})\otimes\mathcal{D}(G_{2}).

  2. (2)

    We have 𝒟​(G)k=0\mathcal{D}(G)_{k}=0 for all k>ν⁡(G)k>\nu(G), where ν⁡(G)\nu(G) is the matching number of GG (that is, the size of a largest matching of GG).

  3. (3)

    We have dim𝒟​(G)1=|V|−c⁡(G)\dim\mathcal{D}(G)_{1}=|V|-c(G), where c⁡(G)c(G) is the number of connected components of GG.

  4. (4)

    If HH is a spanning subgraph of GG, then

    Pk​(H)⊆Pk​(G),dim𝒟​(H)k≤dim𝒟​(G)k.P_{k}(H)\subseteq P_{k}(G),\qquad\dim\mathcal{D}(H)_{k}\leq\dim\mathcal{D}(G)_{k}.

The first assertion follows from the disjoint sets of variables and incidence sums. The second follows from (4). For the third, observe that P1​(G)P_{1}(G) is the span of the vectors xi−xjx_{i}-x_{j}, which are the columns of the incidence matrix of GG; thus, its dimension is the rank of the incidence matrix, which is known to equal |V|−c⁡(G)|V|-c(G). The fourth assertion is immediate (note that there is a graded surjective 𝐤\mathbf{k}-algebra homomorphism 𝒟⁡(G)→𝒟⁡(H)\mathcal{D}(G)\to\mathcal{D}(H) given by sending all ueu_{e} with e∉E⁡(H)e\notin E(H) to 00). ∎

4. Complete graphs and two-row Specht modules

We now specialize to the complete graph KnK_{n} on the vertex set [n][n]. The symmetric group SnS_{n} acts on 𝐤⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbf{k}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] by permuting the variables:

σ⁡(xi)=xσ⁡(i)(σ∈Sn).\sigma(x_{i})=x_{\sigma(i)}\qquad(\sigma\in S_{n}).

Since SnS_{n} also permutes the kk-matchings of KnK_{n}, this action preserves Pk​(Kn)P_{k}(K_{n}): more precisely, σ⁡(pM)=±pσ⁡(M)\sigma(p_{M})=\pm p_{\sigma(M)}, where the sign only reflects our choices of orientations for the edges. Thus Pk​(Kn)P_{k}(K_{n}) is naturally an SnS_{n}-representation.

To identify this representation, let us recall the polynomial realization of the Specht modules. Let λ⊢n\lambda\vdash n, and let TT be a Young tableau of shape λ\lambda, filled bijectively with 1,2,…,n1,2,\ldots,n. For a column of TT whose entries, from top to bottom, are i1,…,iri_{1},\ldots,i_{r}, form the Vandermonde factor

∏1≤a<b≤r(xia−xib).\prod_{1\leq a<b\leq r}(x_{i_{a}}-x_{i_{b}}).

The Specht polynomial of TT is the product of these factors over all columns of TT:

ΔT:=∏column ​C​ of ​T;i1,…,ir​ are the entries of ​C∏1≤a<b≤r(xia−xib).\Delta_{T}:=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{column }C\text{ of }T;\\ i_{1},\ldots,i_{r}\text{ are the entries of }C\end{subarray}}\ \prod_{1\leq a<b\leq r}(x_{i_{a}}-x_{i_{b}}).

The span of the Specht polynomials ΔT\Delta_{T} over all tableaux TT of shape λ\lambda is the usual Specht module SλS^{\lambda}. See, e.g., [27, Satz 1] or [13, Theorem 5.6.1].

Now let λ=(n−k,k)\lambda=(n-k,k), where 0≤k≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor. Such a diagram has exactly kk columns of height 22, while all remaining columns have height 11. Hence every tableau TT of shape (n−k,k)(n-k,k) determines a kk-matching M⁡(T)M(T) of KnK_{n}, namely the pairs of entries occurring in its two-box columns, and we have

ΔT=±pM⁡(T).\Delta_{T}=\pm p_{M(T)}.

Conversely, every kk-matching of KnK_{n} arises in this way from some tableau of shape (n−k,k)(n-k,k). Thus the span Pk​(Kn)P_{k}(K_{n}) of the pMp_{M}’s is precisely the Specht module of shape (n−k,k)(n-k,k).

Theorem 4.1.

For every kk satisfying 0≤k≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor, we have, as SnS_{n}-modules,

Pk​(Kn)≅S(n−k,k).P_{k}(K_{n})\cong S^{(n-k,k)}.

Consequently,

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(Kn),t)=∑0≤k≤n/2((nk)−(nk−1))​tk.\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(K_{n}),t)=\sum_{0\leq k\leq n/2}\left(\binom{n}{k}-\binom{n}{k-1}\right)t^{k}.
Proof.

The SnS_{n}-module identification was established above. For the Hilbert series, we need to compute dimS(n−k,k)\dim S^{(n-k,k)}. Recall that the dimension of any Specht module SλS^{\lambda} equals the number fλf^{\lambda} of all standard Young tableaux of shape λ\lambda, and can be computed by the hook-length formula. Thus,

dimS(n−k,k)=f(n−k,k)=(nk)−(nk−1)=n−2​k+1n−k+1​(nk).\dim S^{(n-k,k)}=f^{(n-k,k)}=\binom{n}{k}-\binom{n}{k-1}=\frac{n-2k+1}{n-k+1}\binom{n}{k}.

Together with (4), this yields the displayed Hilbert series. ∎

Remark 4.2 (Positive characteristic).

The identification Pk​(Kn)≅S(n−k,k)P_{k}(K_{n})\cong S^{(n-k,k)} and the hook length formula for the dimension of the Specht module are valid over any field. However, if 𝐤\mathbf{k} has positive characteristic, then the Specht module can fail to be irreducible. For general graphs, in contrast, even the Hilbert series can depend on the characteristic; see Remark 3.6.

The coefficients of Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(Kn),t)\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(K_{n}),t) form the Catalan triangle and count standard Young tableaux of the fixed shape (n−k,k)(n-k,k).

Remark 4.3 (An exterior analogue).

Assume in this remark that 𝐤\mathbf{k} has characteristic zero. Bergeron, Chan, Soltani, and Zabrocki [3] study a strikingly parallel construction in the exterior algebra

Rn=⋀(ξ1,…,ξn).R_{n}=\bigwedge(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}).

For a matching11 1 They refer to matchings as “pairings”. M={(i1,j1),…,(ik,jk)}M=\{(i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots,(i_{k},j_{k})\} of KnK_{n}, ordered so that j1<⋯<jkj_{1}<\cdots<j_{k} and ir<jri_{r}<j_{r} for every rr, they set

ΔM:=(ξj1−ξi1)⋯(ξjk−ξik)∈Rn.\Delta_{M}:=(\xi_{j_{1}}-\xi_{i_{1}})\cdots(\xi_{j_{k}}-\xi_{i_{k}})\in R_{n}.

They define a specific noncrossing matching C⁡(α)C(\alpha) for each ballot sequence α\alpha. Their Corollary 4.5 shows that the elements ΔC⁡(α)\Delta_{C(\alpha)} indexed by all ballot sequences α\alpha (of length nn with kk entries equal to 11) form a basis of the degree-kk exterior quasisymmetric harmonic space E​Q​Hn,kEQH_{n,k}. Thus,

dimE​Q​Hn,k=f(n−k,k)=dimPk​(Kn).\dim EQH_{n,k}=f^{(n-k,k)}=\dim P_{k}(K_{n}).

There is in fact a very explicit vector-space isomorphism between these two spaces. The same ballot sequences give noncrossing matchings C⁡(α)C(\alpha), and the commutative polynomials pC⁡(α)p_{C(\alpha)} are linearly independent: with respect to the lexicographic order induced by x1>⋯>xnx_{1}>\cdots>x_{n}, the lexicographically smallest monomial of pC⁡(α)p_{C(\alpha)} is obtained by choosing the right endpoint of every pair (i.e., the positions of all closing parentheses), and these monomials are distinct for different α\alpha. Since there are f(n−k,k)f^{(n-k,k)} such ballot sequences, these polynomials form a basis of Pk​(Kn)P_{k}(K_{n}). Hence there is a unique isomorphism

(11) Ψk:Pk​(Kn)⟶E​Q​Hn,k,pC⁡(α)⟼ΔC⁡(α).\Psi_{k}:P_{k}(K_{n})\longrightarrow EQH_{n,k},\qquad p_{C(\alpha)}\longmapsto\Delta_{C(\alpha)}.

So, at the level of graded vector spaces with their preferred noncrossing bases, the commutative and exterior pictures are very close.

However, the parallels end here. The vector space E​Q​Hn,kEQH_{n,k} is the span of the ΔM\Delta_{M} corresponding to all noncrossing matchings MM (by [3, Proposition 2.9 and Corollary 4.5]), but usually not the span of ΔM\Delta_{M} for all the matchings MM. In particular, it is not an SnS_{n}-representation, which should not come as a surprise because the SnS_{n}-action does not preserve noncrossingness (unless k≤1k\leq 1). Thus, there is no hope for an isomorphism of SnS_{n}-representations. 22 2 Another false trail: There is an obvious linear isomorphism from the squarefree degree-kk part of 𝐤⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbf{k}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] to ⋀k𝐤n\bigwedge^{k}\mathbf{k}^{n}, sending xa1⋯xakx_{a_{1}}\cdots x_{a_{k}} (with a1<⋯<aka_{1}<\cdots<a_{k}) to ξa1⋯ξak\xi_{a_{1}}\cdots\xi_{a_{k}}. But this map does not send pMp_{M} to ΔM\Delta_{M}: when the chosen endpoints are reordered, anticommutativity contributes signs which depend on the chosen term of the expansion. Thus, for example, (x1−x4)​(x2−x3)=x1​x2−x1​x3−x2​x4+x3​x4(x_{1}-x_{4})(x_{2}-x_{3})=x_{1}x_{2}-x_{1}x_{3}-x_{2}x_{4}+x_{3}x_{4} is sent to ξ1​ξ2−ξ1​ξ3−ξ2​ξ4+ξ3​ξ4≠(ξ1−ξ4)​(ξ2−ξ3)\xi_{1}\xi_{2}-\xi_{1}\xi_{3}-\xi_{2}\xi_{4}+\xi_{3}\xi_{4}\neq(\xi_{1}-\xi_{4})(\xi_{2}-\xi_{3}).

To drive this point home, let us compare the span of the ΔM\Delta_{M} for all kk-matchings MM of KnK_{n} with E​Q​Hn,kEQH_{n,k}. Let

W=span{ξi−ξj:1≤i,j≤n},W=\operatorname{span}\{\xi_{i}-\xi_{j}:1\leq i,j\leq n\},

the standard (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional representation of SnS_{n}. For a kk-matching MM, the element ΔM\Delta_{M} belongs to the subspace ⋀kW⊆⋀k𝐤n\bigwedge^{k}W\subseteq\bigwedge^{k}\mathbf{k}^{n} (since the kk factors ξjr−ξir\xi_{j_{r}}-\xi_{i_{r}} of ΔM\Delta_{M} all lie in WW), and is nonzero (since the kk factors of ΔM\Delta_{M} are linearly independent). The SnS_{n}-orbit of any one such ΔM\Delta_{M} consists, up to sign, of all ΔN\Delta_{N}s corresponding to all kk-matchings NN. Since the SnS_{n}-representation

⋀kW≅S(n−k,1k)\bigwedge^{k}W\cong S^{(n-k,1^{k})}

is irreducible in characteristic zero, it follows that

(12) span⁡{ΔM:M∈Matchk⁡(Kn)}=⋀kW≅S(n−k,1k).\operatorname{span}\{\Delta_{M}:M\in\operatorname{Match}_{k}(K_{n})\}=\bigwedge^{k}W\cong S^{(n-k,1^{k})}.

Thus the complete commutative matching family {pM:M∈Matchk⁡(Kn)}\{p_{M}:M\in\operatorname{Match}_{k}(K_{n})\} spans the two-row module S(n−k,k)S^{(n-k,k)}, whereas the complete exterior matching family {ΔM:M∈Matchk⁡(Kn)}\{\Delta_{M}:M\in\operatorname{Match}_{k}(K_{n})\} spans the hook module S(n−k,1k)S^{(n-k,1^{k})}. (nk)−(nk−1)and(n−1k),\binom{n}{k}-\binom{n}{k-1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\binom{n-1}{k},
