Already for n=4n=4 and k=2k=2, the difference between the complete commutative and exterior matching families is visible in the Garnir relation

p12​p34−p13​p24+p14​p23=0p_{12}p_{34}-p_{13}p_{24}+p_{14}p_{23}=0

in commuting variables. The three corresponding exterior products are linearly independent (they span ⋀2W\bigwedge^{2}W, which has dimension 33).

Theorem 4.4.

Assume that the field 𝐤\mathbf{k} has characteristic 00. Then, there is an isomorphism of graded algebras

𝒟⁡(Kn)≅𝐤⁡[z1,…,zn]/(z1+⋯+zn,z12,…,zn2),zi⟼θi.\mathcal{D}(K_{n})\cong\mathbf{k}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}]/(z_{1}+\cdots+z_{n},z_{1}^{2},\ldots,z_{n}^{2}),\qquad z_{i}\longmapsto\theta_{i}.

As an abstract commutative algebra, the quotient in Theorem 4.4 is the case q=1q=1 of the family

𝐤⁡[z1,…,zn]/(z12,…,zn2,(z1+⋯+zn)q)\mathbf{k}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}]/(z_{1}^{2},\ldots,z_{n}^{2},(z_{1}+\cdots+z_{n})^{q})

studied in detail by Jonsson Kling et al. [17]; among other things, they determine Gröbner bases and Hilbert series for the general family and give another proof of the strong Lefschetz property of the squarefree algebra. We nevertheless include the short Boolean-lattice argument needed for the present case.

Proof.

The relations in the ideal (z1+⋯+zn,z12,…,zn2)(z_{1}+\cdots+z_{n},z_{1}^{2},\ldots,z_{n}^{2}) hold for the elements θ1,…,θn\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n} by (1), so there is a surjective 𝐤\mathbf{k}-algebra homomorphism

Φ:𝐤⁡[z1,…,zn]/(z1+⋯+zn,z12,…,zn2)→𝒟⁡(Kn)\Phi:\mathbf{k}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}]/(z_{1}+\cdots+z_{n},z_{1}^{2},\ldots,z_{n}^{2})\to\mathcal{D}(K_{n})

that sends each ziz_{i} to θi\theta_{i}. We must show that this surjection Φ\Phi is an isomorphism. It clearly suffices to show that its domain and its codomain have equal Hilbert functions. Put

A:=𝐤⁡[z1,…,zn]/(z12,…,zn2)andL:=z1+⋯+zn∈A.A:=\mathbf{k}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}]/(z_{1}^{2},\ldots,z_{n}^{2})\qquad\text{and}\qquad L:=z_{1}+\cdots+z_{n}\in A.

Note that the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-vector space AA has dimension 2n2^{n} and a basis consisting of the (residue classes of the) squarefree monomials

zS:=∏i∈Szi for all ​S⊆[n].z_{S}:=\prod_{i\in S}z_{i}\qquad\text{ for all }S\subseteq[n].

We must compute the Hilbert function of A/(L)A/(L). This boils down to determining dim(A/(L))k\dim(A/(L))_{k} for all kk. This is rather well-known; indeed, the maximal-rank statement below is the classical Boolean up-operator phenomenon underlying the strong Lefschetz property of this squarefree complete intersection; see also Stanley [28] and [17, §3.1]. We give the elementary argument here for the sake of completeness. We claim that multiplication by LL – that is, the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-linear map

Ur:Ar⟶Ar+1,f⟼L​fU_{r}:A_{r}\longrightarrow A_{r+1},\qquad f\longmapsto Lf

– has maximal rank in every degree (i.e., is injective for r<n/2r<n/2 and surjective for r≥n/2r\geq n/2). It is enough to prove this over ℝ\mathbb{R}. Indeed, in the squarefree monomial bases, the matrix of UrU_{r} has only 00’s and 11’s, so a maximal minor which is nonzero over ℝ\mathbb{R} is a nonzero integer and therefore remains nonzero over every field of characteristic zero.

The maps Ur:Ar→Ar+1U_{r}:A_{r}\to A_{r+1} for all rr are the graded pieces of a 𝐤\mathbf{k}-linear map U:A→AU:A\to A, which we call the up-operator since it raises degrees by 11. Define the down-operator D:A→AD:A\to A as the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-linear map given by

D⁡(zS):=∑i∈SzS∖{i} for each ​S⊆[n].D(z_{S}):=\sum_{i\in S}z_{S\setminus\{i\}}\qquad\text{ for each }S\subseteq[n].

This operator decreases degrees by 11; that is, D⁡(Ar)⊆Ar−1D(A_{r})\subseteq A_{r-1} for each rr.

Give the ℝ\mathbb{R}-vector space AA the inner product for which the squarefree monomials zSz_{S} are orthonormal. Then DD is the adjoint of UU. A direct calculation gives, on ArA_{r}, the equality

(13) D​U−U​D=(n−2​r)​idAr.DU-UD=(n-2r)\,\operatorname{id}_{A_{r}}.

Indeed, for |S|=r|S|=r, the mixed terms zS∖{i}∪{j}z_{S\setminus\{i\}\cup\{j\}} occur once in both D​U​(zS)DU(z_{S}) and U​D​(zS)UD(z_{S}), while zSz_{S} occurs respectively n−rn-r and rr times.

If r<n/2r<n/2 and 0≠f∈Ar0\neq f\in A_{r}, then

‖U​f‖2\displaystyle\|Uf\|^{2} =⟨Uf,Uf⟩=⟨DUf,f⟩(since D and U are adjoint)\displaystyle=\langle Uf,Uf\rangle=\langle DUf,f\rangle\qquad\left(\text{since $D$ and $U$ are adjoint}\right)
=⟨UDf+(n−2r)f,f⟩(since DU=UD+(n−2r)idAr by (13))\displaystyle=\langle UDf+(n-2r)f,f\rangle\qquad\left(\text{since }DU=UD+(n-2r)\,\operatorname{id}_{A_{r}}\text{ by }\eqref{eq:boolean-commutator}\right)
=⟨U​D​f,f⟩+(n−2​r)​‖f‖2\displaystyle=\langle UDf,f\rangle+(n-2r)\|f\|^{2}
=∥Df∥2+(n−2r)∥f∥2(again since D and U are adjoint)\displaystyle=\|Df\|^{2}+(n-2r)\|f\|^{2}\qquad\left(\text{again since $D$ and $U$ are adjoint}\right)
>0(by positive definiteness and since n−2​r>0),\displaystyle>0\qquad\left(\text{by positive definiteness and since $n-2r>0$}\right),

whence U​f≠0Uf\neq 0. Thus UrU_{r} is injective on the lower half of AA (that is, for r<n/2r<n/2). On the other hand, the adjoint of UrU_{r} with respect to our inner product is Dr+1:Ar+1→ArD_{r+1}:A_{r+1}\to A_{r} (that is, the restriction of DD to Ar+1A_{r+1}); thus, the injectivity of UrU_{r} for r<n/2r<n/2 entails the surjectivity of its adjoint Dr+1D_{r+1} for r<n/2r<n/2. Under the complement identification zS↔z[n]∖Sz_{S}\leftrightarrow z_{[n]\setminus S}, this down-operator Dr+1D_{r+1} becomes Un−r−1U_{n-r-1} (to make this more precise: we have Un−r−1=Xr∘Dr+1∘Xr+1−1U_{n-r-1}=X_{r}\circ D_{r+1}\circ X_{r+1}^{-1}, where XkX_{k} denotes the isomorphism Ak→An−kA_{k}\to A_{n-k} sending each zSz_{S} to z[n]∖Sz_{[n]\setminus S}). Hence the surjectivity of Dr+1D_{r+1} we just proved entails that Un−r−1U_{n-r-1} is surjective for r<n/2r<n/2. Substituting n−r−1n-r-1 for rr here, we conclude that UrU_{r} is surjective for all r>n/2−1r>n/2-1, hence in particular for all r≥n/2r\geq n/2.

Thus we have shown that UrU_{r} is injective whenever r<n/2r<n/2 and surjective whenever r≥n/2r\geq n/2. Hence, UrU_{r} always has maximal rank:

rank⁡Ur=min⁡{dimAr,dimAr+1}=min⁡{(nr),(nr+1)}\operatorname{rank}U_{r}=\min\left\{\dim A_{r},\dim A_{r+1}\right\}=\min\left\{\binom{n}{r},\binom{n}{r+1}\right\}

(since dimAk=(nk)\dim A_{k}=\binom{n}{k}). This proves the claim.

For k=0k=0, we plainly have dim(A/(L))0=1\dim(A/(L))_{0}=1. Now let k≥1k\geq 1. Since dimAk=(nk)\dim A_{k}=\binom{n}{k}, the claim we just proved shows that

rank⁡Uk−1=min⁡{(nk−1),(nk)}.\operatorname{rank}U_{k-1}=\min\left\{\binom{n}{k-1},\binom{n}{k}\right\}.

But the degree-kk component of A/(L)A/(L) is the cokernel of Uk−1:Ak−1→AkU_{k-1}:A_{k-1}\to A_{k}. Therefore

dim(A/(L))k\displaystyle\dim(A/(L))_{k} =(nk)−rank⁡Uk−1=(nk)−min⁡{(nk−1),(nk)}\displaystyle=\binom{n}{k}-\operatorname{rank}U_{k-1}=\binom{n}{k}-\min\left\{\binom{n}{k-1},\binom{n}{k}\right\}
=max⁡{(nk)−(nk−1),0}.\displaystyle=\max\left\{\binom{n}{k}-\binom{n}{k-1},0\right\}.

This agrees with dim𝒟​(Kn)k\dim\mathcal{D}(K_{n})_{k} by Theorem 4.1. The surjection Φ\Phi is therefore an isomorphism in every degree (since a surjective linear map between finite-dimensional vector spaces of the same dimension must be an isomorphism). ∎

Remark 4.5 (The presentation in positive characteristic).

The characteristic-zero hypothesis in Theorem 4.4 is crucial. Over an arbitrary field, the same assignment zi↦θiz_{i}\mapsto\theta_{i} gives a graded surjection

Φ:𝐤⁡[z1,…,zn]/(z1+⋯+zn,z12,…,zn2)⟶𝒟⁡(Kn).\Phi:\mathbf{k}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}]/(z_{1}+\cdots+z_{n},z_{1}^{2},\ldots,z_{n}^{2})\longrightarrow\mathcal{D}(K_{n}).

Suppose now that char⁡𝐤=p>0\operatorname{char}\mathbf{k}=p>0. In the squarefree monomial bases, the map

Ur:Ar⟶Ar+1U_{r}:A_{r}\longrightarrow A_{r+1}

is the inclusion matrix between the rr-subsets and the (r+1)(r+1)-subsets of [n][n]. Wilson’s diagonal form for inclusion matrices [29] shows, when r<n/2r<n/2, that its nonzero diagonal entries over ℤ\mathbb{Z} are

1,2,…,r+1(with positive multiplicities).1,2,\ldots,r+1\qquad\left(\text{with positive multiplicities}\right).

Hence UrU_{r} is injective over 𝐤\mathbf{k} if and only if p>r+1p>r+1. By complementing subsets, the corresponding statement in the upper half is equivalent to surjectivity. Consequently all the maps UrU_{r} have maximal rank if and only if

p>⌈n2⌉.p>\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil.

Since Theorem 4.1 shows that the Hilbert series of 𝒟⁡(Kn)\mathcal{D}(K_{n}) itself is independent of the characteristic, the surjection Φ\Phi above is an isomorphism exactly when

p>⌈n2⌉;p>\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil;

for p≤⌈n/2⌉p\leq\lceil n/2\rceil, its source has a larger Hilbert function than 𝒟⁡(Kn)\mathcal{D}(K_{n}) in at least one degree.

5. Arbitrary graphs

We begin with conventions. For a finite set WW, let KWK_{W} denote the complete graph with vertex set WW. Thus K[n]=KnK_{[n]}=K_{n}. The graphs KnK_{n} and KWK_{W} are isomorphic whenever |W|=n\left|W\right|=n; thus, they differ only in the labeling of the vertices. Thus, for the rest of this section, we assume that the vertex set VV of our graph GG is [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}, but we expect the reader to understand that all our results hold equally well, after relabeling, for graphs on any other nn-element vertex set.

The spaces Pk​(G)P_{k}(G) can be computed in finite time: enumerate the kk-matchings, expand their products in the monomial basis of 𝐤​[xv]k\mathbf{k}[x_{v}]_{k}, and take their span (which is the column space of a matrix). In particular, Pk​(G)⊆Pk​(Kn)P_{k}(G)\subseteq P_{k}(K_{n}), since GG is a subgraph of KnK_{n}. We may wonder when equality holds:

Definition 5.1.

Let 0≤k≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor. We say that a graph GG on nn vertices is kk-saturated if

Pk​(G)=Pk​(Kn).P_{k}(G)=P_{k}(K_{n}).
Problem 5.2.

Characterize the kk-saturated graphs, either for a prescribed kk or simultaneously for all k≤ν⁡(G)k\leq\nu(G).

Note that this question can be restated as a question about the Specht generators ΔT\Delta_{T} of the Specht module S(n−k,k)S^{(n-k,k)}: namely, we ask whether the subcollection selected by the kk-matchings of GG spans the whole Specht module. In contrast, the Specht matroid introduced by Wiltshire-Gordon, Woo, and Zajaczkowska [30] records the linear dependences among the classical Specht generators of a given Specht module SλS^{\lambda}.

5.1. The elementary Garnir relations

The elementary Garnir relations already give useful information. For any two vertices ii and jj, write pi​j=xi−xjp_{ij}=x_{i}-x_{j}, so that pj​i=−pi​jp_{ji}=-p_{ij}.

Lemma 5.3 (Elementary Garnir relations).

Let NN be a matching of GG, and a,b,c,da,b,c,d be four vertices. Then

(14) pN​(pa​b+pb​c+pc​a)\displaystyle p_{N}(p_{ab}+p_{bc}+p_{ca}) =0,\displaystyle=0,
(15) pN​(pa​b​pc​d−pa​c​pb​d+pa​d​pb​c)\displaystyle p_{N}(p_{ab}p_{cd}-p_{ac}p_{bd}+p_{ad}p_{bc}) =0.\displaystyle=0.
Proof.

Both identities follow by expanding pi​j=xi−xjp_{ij}=x_{i}-x_{j}. ∎

When the vertices a,b,c,da,b,c,d in Lemma 5.3 are distinct and are not incident to any edge of NN, the equalities (14) and (15) are linear relations among matching generators of P|N|+1​(Kn)P_{|N|+1}(K_{n}) and P|N|+2​(Kn)P_{|N|+2}(K_{n}), respectively. These are precisely the three-vertex and four-vertex straightening relations for the two-row Specht polynomial model.

5.2. kk-saturation implies kk-connectivity

The first general obstruction is connectivity. We say that GG is kk-connected if GG has more than kk vertices and the graph G−SG-S is connected for every set S⊂VS\subset V with |S|<k|S|<k. (In particular, the graph GG is 22-connected if it is connected, has at least three vertices and has no cut-vertex.)

Proposition 5.4 (Connectivity obstruction).

Let 1≤k≤⌊n/2⌋1\leq k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor. If GG is kk-saturated, then GG is kk-connected.

Proof.

Suppose that S⊂VS\subset V has size s<ks<k and that G−SG-S has at least two components C1,…,CmC_{1},\ldots,C_{m}. In the polynomial ring R=𝐤[xv:v∈V]R=\mathbf{k}[x_{v}:v\in V], define the ideal

J=(xu−xv:u,v∈Ci for some i).J=(x_{u}-x_{v}:u,v\in C_{i}\text{ for some }i).

The quotient R/JR/J is a polynomial ring with one variable for each CiC_{i} and one variable for each vertex of SS. Hence a linear factor pu​vp_{uv} belongs to JJ exactly when uu and vv lie in the same component CiC_{i}.

Every kk-matching of GG has at most ss edges incident with SS. All its remaining edges lie inside the components CiC_{i}, so

(16) pM∈Jk−sfor each ​M∈Matchk⁡(G).\displaystyle p_{M}\in J^{k-s}\qquad\text{for each }M\in\operatorname{Match}_{k}(G).

Thus Pk​(G)⊆Jk−sP_{k}(G)\subseteq J^{k-s}.

On the other hand, choose vertices c1∈C1c_{1}\in C_{1} and c2∈C2c_{2}\in C_{2}. Since n≥2​kn\geq 2k and s<ks<k, we have s≤n−s−2s\leq n-s-2, so there are enough further vertices outside SS to pair each vertex of SS with a distinct vertex outside S∪{c1,c2}S\cup\{c_{1},c_{2}\}. Together with the edge c1​c2c_{1}c_{2}, these give s+1s+1 pairwise disjoint edges of KnK_{n} whose linear factors xi−xjx_{i}-x_{j} do not belong to JJ. Complete them arbitrarily to a kk-matching QQ of KnK_{n}. We shall show that pQ∉Jk−sp_{Q}\notin J^{k-s}.

Choose one vertex ci∈Cic_{i}\in C_{i} in each component and use the coordinates

zi:=xci,yu:=xu−xci(for u∈Ci∖{ci}),z_{i}:=x_{c_{i}},\qquad y_{u}:=x_{u}-x_{c_{i}}\quad(\text{for }u\in C_{i}\setminus\{c_{i}\}),

together with the variables xsx_{s} for s∈Ss\in S. In these coordinates

R=𝐤⁡[z1,…,zm,xs​(s∈S),yu],J=(yu).R=\mathbf{k}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{m},\ x_{s}\ (s\in S),\ y_{u}],\qquad J=(y_{u}).

Introduce an auxiliary variable tt and define the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-algebra morphism σt:R→R⁡[t]\sigma_{t}:R\to R[t] that fixes the ziz_{i} and the xsx_{s} and sends every yuy_{u} to t​yuty_{u}. If f∈Jdf\in J^{d}, then σt​(f)\sigma_{t}(f) is divisible by tdt^{d}.

For a linear factor pu​v=xu−xvp_{uv}=x_{u}-x_{v}, the polynomial σt​(pu​v)\sigma_{t}(p_{uv}) is divisible by tt exactly when uu and vv lie in the same component CiC_{i}; in that case it is divisible by tt exactly once. Otherwise its constant term at t=0t=0 is a nonzero linear form in the ziz_{i} and xsx_{s}. Since the polynomial ring is a domain, the tt-adic order of a product of such factors is exactly the number of factors that belong to JJ.

The matching QQ contains the s+1s+1 chosen edges whose factors are not in JJ, so at most k−s−1k-s-1 of its factors belong to JJ. Hence σt​(pQ)\sigma_{t}(p_{Q}) is not divisible by tk−st^{k-s}, and therefore

pQ∉Jk−s.p_{Q}\notin J^{k-s}.

Thus, Pk​(Kn)⊈Jk−sP_{k}(K_{n})\nsubseteq J^{k-s} (since pQ∈Pk​(Kn)p_{Q}\in P_{k}(K_{n})). Contrasting this with Pk​(G)⊆Jk−sP_{k}(G)\subseteq J^{k-s}, we obtain Pk​(G)≠Pk​(Kn)P_{k}(G)\neq P_{k}(K_{n}), which contradicts the assumption that GG be kk-saturated. This is the contradiction we need to complete our proof.

(The above argument using σt\sigma_{t} resembles the use of Rees algebras in the study of ideal powers.) ∎

For k≥3k\geq 3, kk-connectivity is not sufficient.

Example 5.5.

Let GG be the triangular prism. It is 33-connected, but it has only four perfect matchings. Hence

dimP3​(G)≤4<5=(63)−(62)=dimP3​(K6),\dim P_{3}(G)\leq 4<5=\binom{6}{3}-\binom{6}{2}=\dim P_{3}(K_{6}),

so GG is not 33-saturated.

5.3. 22-connectivity implies 22-saturation

In degree 22 the connectivity obstruction is sharp. To prove this, we need some lemmas:

Lemma 5.6 (Two-row branching sequence).

Let VV be a finite set with |V|≥4|V|\geq 4, let v∈Vv\in V, and put V′:=V∖{v}V^{\prime}:=V\setminus\{v\}. Every element of P2​(KV)P_{2}(K_{V}) is at most linear in xvx_{v}, so coefficient extraction at xvx_{v} defines a map [xv]:P2​(KV)→P1​(KV′)[x_{v}]:P_{2}(K_{V})\to P_{1}(K_{V^{\prime}}). There is a short exact sequence

(17) 0⟶P2​(KV′)⟶P2​(KV)→[xv]P1​(KV′)⟶0,0\longrightarrow P_{2}(K_{V^{\prime}})\longrightarrow P_{2}(K_{V})\xrightarrow{[x_{v}]}P_{1}(K_{V^{\prime}})\longrightarrow 0,

where the first (nonzero) map is the evident inclusion.

Proof.

The first map is injective, and its image lies in the kernel of the last map. The last map is surjective: for distinct c,d∈V′c,d\in V^{\prime}, choose a∈V′∖{c,d}a\in V^{\prime}\setminus\{c,d\}; then, up to sign,

[xv]​(pv​a​pc​d)=pc​d.[x_{v}](p_{va}p_{cd})=p_{cd}.

The dimension formula in Theorem 4.1 gives

dimP2​(KV)−dimP2​(KV′)=|V|−2=dimP1​(KV′),\dim P_{2}(K_{V})-\dim P_{2}(K_{V^{\prime}})=|V|-2=\dim P_{1}(K_{V^{\prime}}),

so that dimP2​(KV)=dimP2​(KV′)+dimP1​(KV′)\dim P_{2}(K_{V})=\dim P_{2}(K_{V^{\prime}})+\dim P_{1}(K_{V^{\prime}}). All that remains is to apply the easy linear-algebraic lemma saying that if

0⟶A​⟶𝑓​B​⟶𝑔​C⟶00\longrightarrow A\overset{f}{\longrightarrow}B\overset{g}{\longrightarrow}C\longrightarrow 0

is a complex of finite-dimensional vector spaces such that ff is injective and gg is surjective and dimB=dimA+dimC\dim B=\dim A+\dim C, then this complex is exact. ∎

Lemma 5.7 (A degree-two vertex).

Every finite 22-connected graph contains a spanning subgraph that is edge-minimal subject to being 22-connected. Every such edge-minimal subgraph has a vertex of degree 22.

Proof.

The first assertion follows simply by deleting edges as long as 22-connectivity is preserved. For the second we use the standard ear characterization of 22-connected graphs; see [20, Theorem 25.4]. Let R1,…,RqR_{1},\ldots,R_{q} be an ear decomposition of the edge-minimal graph HH. If HH is a cycle, every vertex has degree 22. Otherwise, the final ear RqR_{q} cannot have length 11: deleting that one edge would leave the union of the preceding ears, which is still a spanning 22-connected graph. Thus RqR_{q} has an internal vertex. Since no later ear exists, every internal vertex of RqR_{q} has degree exactly 22 in HH. ∎

Lemma 5.8 (Suppressing a degree-two vertex).

Let HH be a 22-connected graph with |V⁡(H)|≥4|V(H)|\geq 4, and let v∈V⁡(H)v\in V(H) have degree 22, with neighbors a,ba,b. Put V′:=V⁡(H)∖{v}V^{\prime}:=V(H)\setminus\{v\} and

H+:=(H−v)+a​b,H−:=H+−a​b=(H−v)−a​b.H^{+}:=(H-v)+ab,\qquad H^{-}:=H^{+}-ab=(H-v)-ab.

Thus H−H^{-} is obtained from H−vH-v by deleting a​bab if that edge was already present; if a​b∉E⁡(H−v)ab\notin E(H-v), then simply H−=H−vH^{-}=H-v. Then H+H^{+} is 22-connected and H−H^{-} is connected.

Proof.

First consider H+H^{+}. It has at least three vertices. Let w∈V′w\in V^{\prime}. We claim that H+−wH^{+}-w is connected. Indeed, given two vertices of H+−wH^{+}-w, choose a path between them in H−wH-w. If this path uses vv, then vv is an internal vertex of the path, so both neighbors a,ba,b of vv are present in H−wH-w (since aa and bb are the only neighbors of vv in HH), and the path uses the segment a−v−ba-v-b (or b−v−ab-v-a). Replacing this segment by the edge a​bab gives a path in H+−wH^{+}-w connecting the same two vertices. Thus H+−wH^{+}-w is connected. Hence deletion of any vertex leaves H+H^{+} connected, so H+H^{+} is 22-connected.

Now consider H−H^{-}. Since HH is 22-connected, H−vH-v is connected. If a​b∉E⁡(H−v)ab\notin E(H-v), there is nothing more to prove. Suppose instead that a​b∈E⁡(H−v)ab\in E(H-v) and that deleting a​bab disconnects H−vH-v. Then a​bab is a bridge of H−vH-v. Let AA and BB be the two components of (H−v)−a​b(H-v)-ab, with a∈Aa\in A and b∈Bb\in B. If A≠{a}A\neq\{a\}, then in H−aH-a the nonempty set A∖{a}A\setminus\{a\} has no edge to the rest of the graph: there is no such edge in H−v−a​bH-v-ab, and the only edges incident with vv are a​vav and b​vbv. This contradicts the connectedness of H−aH-a. Hence A={a}A=\{a\}, and similarly B={b}B=\{b\}. Thus V⁡(H)={a,b,v}V(H)=\{a,b,v\}, contradicting |V⁡(H)|≥4|V(H)|\geq 4. Therefore H−H^{-} is connected.

For example, if H=C4H=C_{4} and vv is any vertex, then its neighbors a,ba,b are not adjacent in HH. Thus H−vH-v is a three-vertex path, H+H^{+} is a triangle, and H−=H−vH^{-}=H-v is that same path. ∎

Theorem 5.9 (Degree-two saturation).

Let GG be a graph on n≥4n\geq 4 vertices. Then

P2(G)=P2(Kn)⟺G is 2-connected.P_{2}(G)=P_{2}(K_{n})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G\text{ is $2$-connected}.
Proof.

The forward implication is Proposition 5.4. Conversely, let GG be 22-connected and choose, by Lemma 5.7, a spanning edge-minimal 22-connected subgraph H⊆GH\subseteq G and a degree-22 vertex vv of HH, with neighbors a,ba,b. Put V′:=V∖{v}V^{\prime}:=V\setminus\{v\} and

H+=(H−v)+a​b,H−=(H−v)−a​b.H^{+}=(H-v)+ab,\qquad H^{-}=(H-v)-ab.

By Lemma 5.8, H+H^{+} is 22-connected and H−H^{-} is connected. If |V′|=3|V^{\prime}|=3, then H+=KV′H^{+}=K_{V^{\prime}}; otherwise induction on nn gives

P2​(H+)=P2​(KV′).P_{2}(H^{+})=P_{2}(K_{V^{\prime}}).

We want to prove that P2​(G)=P2​(Kn)P_{2}(G)=P_{2}(K_{n}). Since P2​(H)⊆P2​(G)⊆P2​(KV)=P2​(Kn)P_{2}(H)\subseteq P_{2}(G)\subseteq P_{2}(K_{V})=P_{2}(K_{n}), it is enough to prove P2​(H)=P2​(KV)P_{2}(H)=P_{2}(K_{V}).

Recall the elementary linear-algebra fact that if

0⟶A⟶B⟶C⟶00\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow B\longrightarrow C\longrightarrow 0

is a short exact sequence of vector spaces, and if W⊆BW\subseteq B is a subspace that contains AA and surjects onto CC, then W=BW=B. Applying this to the short exact sequence (17) and the subspace P2​(H)P_{2}(H) of P2​(KV)P_{2}(K_{V}), we see that it suffices to show that P2​(H)P_{2}(H) contains P2​(KV′)P_{2}(K_{V^{\prime}}) and surjects onto P1​(KV′)P_{1}(K_{V^{\prime}}) under [xv][x_{v}].

We start with the first claim. Since P2​(H+)=P2​(KV′)P_{2}(H^{+})=P_{2}(K_{V^{\prime}}), it is enough to show that every matching polynomial pM∈P2​(H+)p_{M}\in P_{2}(H^{+}) belongs to P2​(H)P_{2}(H). So consider a 22-matching MM of H+H^{+}. If a​b∉Mab\notin M, then MM is already a 22-matching of HH, and thus pM∈P2​(H)p_{M}\in P_{2}(H) follows. If a​b∈Mab\in M, then we let c​dcd be the other edge of MM (so pM=pa​b​pc​dp_{M}=p_{ab}p_{cd}); then, the triangle Garnir relation (14) gives

pa​b​pc​d=(pa​v+pv​b)​pc​d=pa​v​pc​d+pv​b​pc​d,p_{ab}p_{cd}=(p_{av}+p_{vb})p_{cd}=p_{av}p_{cd}+p_{vb}p_{cd},

and both terms on the right come from 22-matchings of HH, so the sum again belongs to P2​(H)P_{2}(H). Hence

P2​(KV′)=P2​(H+)⊆P2​(H).P_{2}(K_{V^{\prime}})=P_{2}(H^{+})\subseteq P_{2}(H).

It remains to prove the surjection claim. For every edge c​dcd of the connected graph H−H^{-}, at least one of a,ba,b is not incident with c​dcd. Pairing c​dcd with the corresponding edge a​vav or b​vbv gives a 22-matching of HH whose xvx_{v}-coefficient is, up to sign, pc​dp_{cd}. Thus, pc​d∈[xv]​P2​(H)p_{cd}\in[x_{v}]P_{2}(H). Therefore

[xv]​P2​(H)⊇P1​(H−)=P1​(KV′),[x_{v}]P_{2}(H)\supseteq P_{1}(H^{-})=P_{1}(K_{V^{\prime}}),

where the last equality follows from the connectivity of H−H^{-}. That is, P2​(H)P_{2}(H) surjects onto P1​(KV′)P_{1}(K_{V^{\prime}}) under [xv][x_{v}]. The preceding linear-algebra observation now yields P2​(H)=P2​(KV)P_{2}(H)=P_{2}(K_{V}), and hence P2​(G)=P2​(Kn)P_{2}(G)=P_{2}(K_{n}). ∎

5.4. kk-linkedness implies kk-saturation

There is also a simple sufficient condition in every degree.

Definition 5.10.

A graph GG is kk-linked if, whenever a1,b1,…,ak,bka_{1},b_{1},\ldots,a_{k},b_{k} are distinct vertices, there exist pairwise vertex-disjoint paths QiQ_{i} joining aia_{i} to bib_{i} for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k. (Paths are defined with respect to the undirected graph GG; they need not conform with the orientation we chose for the edges.)

Proposition 5.11 (Linkedness criterion).

If GG is kk-linked, then GG is kk-saturated.

Proof.

Take an arbitrary kk-matching M={{a1,b1},…,{ak,bk}}M=\{\{a_{1},b_{1}\},\ldots,\{a_{k},b_{k}\}\} of KnK_{n}, and choose pairwise vertex-disjoint paths QiQ_{i} in GG joining aia_{i} to bib_{i}. Along each path,

xai−xbi=∑u​v∈E⁡(Qi)εu​v​(xu−xv),εu​v∈{±1}.x_{a_{i}}-x_{b_{i}}=\sum_{uv\in E(Q_{i})}\varepsilon_{uv}(x_{u}-x_{v}),\qquad\varepsilon_{uv}\in\{\pm 1\}.

Multiplying these kk identities expresses pMp_{M} as a linear combination of products obtained by choosing one edge from each QiQ_{i}. Since the paths are vertex-disjoint, every such choice is a kk-matching of GG. Hence pM∈Pk​(G)p_{M}\in P_{k}(G). Thus Pk​(Kn)⊆Pk​(G)P_{k}(K_{n})\subseteq P_{k}(G), and the result follows. ∎

Thus, for 1≤k≤⌊n/2⌋1\leq k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor, we have the useful chain

k​-linked⟹k​-saturated⟹k​-connected.k\text{-linked}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k\text{-saturated}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad k\text{-connected}.

The second implication is an equivalence for k=1,2k=1,2, but Example 5.5 shows that it is not an equivalence for k=3k=3.

5.5. Matching-complement implies kk-saturation

The Garnir relations also settle another useful family of graphs.

Theorem 5.12 (Matching-complement saturation).

Let GG be a graph on n≥3n\geq 3 vertices whose complement G¯\overline{G} is a matching. Then GG is kk-saturated for every 0≤k≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor.

Proof.

Call the edges of G¯\overline{G} forbidden. We must show that pM∈Pk​(G)p_{M}\in P_{k}(G) for each kk-matching MM of KnK_{n}. We shall show this by strong induction on the number of forbidden edges in MM. There is nothing to prove if MM contains no forbidden edge. Suppose that a​b∈Mab\in M is forbidden.

If 2​k<n2k<n, choose an unmatched vertex cc. Since the forbidden edges form a matching, both a​cac and c​bcb are edges of GG. The triangle relation (14) gives

pa​b=pa​c+pc​b.p_{ab}=p_{ac}+p_{cb}.

After multiplication by the factors belonging to M∖{a​b}M\setminus\{ab\}, this expresses pMp_{M} as a sum of two matching polynomials pNp_{N} and pRp_{R} where NN and RR each have one fewer forbidden edge than MM. By induction, this shows that pM∈Pk​(G)p_{M}\in P_{k}(G).

If 2​k=n2k=n, then n≥4n\geq 4 and k≥2k\geq 2. Choose another edge c​d∈Mcd\in M. Again the matching condition on G¯\overline{G} implies that all four cross edges a​c,a​d,b​c,b​dac,ad,bc,bd belong to GG. The four-vertex Garnir relation (15) gives

pa​b​pc​d=pa​c​pb​d−pa​d​pb​c.p_{ab}p_{cd}=p_{ac}p_{bd}-p_{ad}p_{bc}.

Multiplying by the remaining factors again decreases the number of forbidden edges (by 11 or by 22). Induction completes the proof. ∎

Corollary 5.13 (Multipartite saturation).

Let r≥2r\geq 2 and let

G=K2,…,2G=K_{2,\ldots,2}

be the complete rr-partite graph with all rr parts of size 22. Then

Pk​(G)=Pk​(K2​r) for all ​0≤k≤r,P_{k}(G)=P_{k}(K_{2r})\qquad\text{ for all }0\leq k\leq r,

and therefore

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)=∑k=0r((2​rk)−(2​rk−1))​tk.\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)=\sum_{k=0}^{r}\left(\binom{2r}{k}-\binom{2r}{k-1}\right)t^{k}.
Proof.

The complement of K2,…,2K_{2,\ldots,2} is the perfect matching consisting of the rr within-part pairs, so Theorem 5.12 applies. The Hilbert series then follows from Theorem 4.1. ∎

Remark 5.14.

The restriction r≥2r\geq 2 is necessary: for r=1r=1 the graph has two vertices and no edges, so it is not saturated in degree 11.

For r=5r=5, Corollary 5.13 gives

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)=1+9​t+35​t2+75​t3+90​t4+42​t5.\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)=1+9t+35t^{2}+75t^{3}+90t^{4}+42t^{5}.

5.6. Matching-equivalent graphs

The matching numbers mk​(G)m_{k}(G) of GG are the coefficients of the Hilbert series of ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G), but they do not determine the Hilbert series of 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G). Let us see when they do agree:

Proposition 5.15 (Forests).

For every graph GG, we have the equivalence

𝒟(G)=ℳ(G)⟺G is a forest.\mathcal{D}(G)=\mathcal{M}(G)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G\text{ is a forest}.

Consequently, if GG is a forest, then

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)=∑k≥0mk​(G)​tk.\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)=\sum_{k\geq 0}m_{k}(G)t^{k}.
Proof.

The degree-one part 𝒟​(G)1\mathcal{D}(G)_{1} is the row space of an oriented incidence matrix of GG, whereas ℳ​(G)1\mathcal{M}(G)_{1} has the edge generators ueu_{e} as a basis. Hence

dim𝒟​(G)1=|V|−c⁡(G),dimℳ​(G)1=|E|.\dim\mathcal{D}(G)_{1}=|V|-c(G),\qquad\dim\mathcal{M}(G)_{1}=|E|.

If GG is a forest, then |E|=|V|−c⁡(G)|E|=|V|-c(G), so the incidence rows span all of ℳ​(G)1\mathcal{M}(G)_{1}. Thus every generator ueu_{e} belongs to 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G), and therefore 𝒟⁡(G)=ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G)=\mathcal{M}(G). Conversely, equality of the two algebras implies equality in degree one, hence |E|=|V|−c⁡(G)|E|=|V|-c(G), which is equivalent to every connected component of GG being a tree. ∎

For brevity, write

𝔪G​(t):=∑k≥0mk​(G)​tk\mathfrak{m}_{G}(t):=\sum_{k\geq 0}m_{k}(G)t^{k}

for the matching generating polynomial of GG. The next result shows explicitly what information beyond 𝔪G​(t)\mathfrak{m}_{G}(t) can enter even when GG has only one cycle. We recall that a graph is said to be unicyclic if it is connected and has exactly one cycle. Equivalently, a unicyclic graph is a graph obtained by adding an edge to a tree. Thus, any unicyclic graph has equally many vertices and edges.

Theorem 5.16 (Unicyclic graphs).

Let GG be a unicyclic graph, let CC be its unique cycle, and put F:=G−V⁡(C)F:=G-V(C). Choose signs ϵe∈{±1}\epsilon_{e}\in\{\pm 1\}, for e∈Ce\in C, such that

∑e∈Cϵe​pe=0,\sum_{e\in C}\epsilon_{e}p_{e}=0,

and put

cC:=∑e∈Cϵe​ue∈ℳ⁡(G).c_{C}:=\sum_{e\in C}\epsilon_{e}u_{e}\in\mathcal{M}(G).

Also set

𝒫⁡(G):=⨁k≥0Pk​(G),\mathcal{P}(G):=\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}P_{k}(G),

regarded only as a graded vector space, and let

ρG:ℳ⁡(G)⟶𝒫⁡(G),uM⟼pM\rho_{G}:\mathcal{M}(G)\longrightarrow\mathcal{P}(G),\qquad u_{M}\longmapsto p_{M}

be the graded linear map defined on the matching basis of ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G). Then there is a short exact sequence of graded vector spaces

(18) 0⟶ℳ⁡(F)​(−1)→⋅cCℳ⁡(G)→ρG𝒫⁡(G)⟶0.0\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}(F)(-1)\xrightarrow{\ \cdot c_{C}\ }\mathcal{M}(G)\xrightarrow{\ \rho_{G}\ }\mathcal{P}(G)\longrightarrow 0.

Here ℳ⁡(F)​(−1)k=ℳ​(F)k−1\mathcal{M}(F)(-1)_{k}=\mathcal{M}(F)_{k-1}.

Consequently, with the convention m−1​(F)=0m_{-1}(F)=0, we have

dimPk​(G)=mk​(G)−mk−1​(F) for all ​k≥0,\dim P_{k}(G)=m_{k}(G)-m_{k-1}(F)\qquad\text{ for all }k\geq 0,

or equivalently,

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)=𝔪G​(t)−t​𝔪F​(t).\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)=\mathfrak{m}_{G}(t)-t\mathfrak{m}_{F}(t).
Proof.

The first map in (18) is well defined because every edge of FF is disjoint from every edge of CC. Now, we shall show that it is injective.

Indeed, for any matching NN of FF, we have

cC​uN=∑e∈Cϵe​ue​uN=∑e∈Cϵe​uN∪{e}.c_{C}u_{N}=\sum_{e\in C}\epsilon_{e}u_{e}u_{N}=\sum_{e\in C}\epsilon_{e}u_{N\cup\{e\}}.

Thus, for any z=∑NaN​uN∈ℳ⁡(F)z=\sum_{N}a_{N}u_{N}\in\mathcal{M}(F), we have

cC​z=∑N∑e∈CaN​ϵe​uN∪{e},c_{C}z=\sum_{N}\sum_{e\in C}a_{N}\epsilon_{e}u_{N\cup\{e\}},

and all the matchings N∪{e}N\cup\{e\} in this double sum are distinct. Thus the coefficient of uN∪{e}u_{N\cup\{e\}} in cC​zc_{C}z is aN​ϵea_{N}\epsilon_{e}. Since ϵe≠0\epsilon_{e}\neq 0, the equality cC​z=0c_{C}z=0 therefore forces aN=0a_{N}=0 for every NN. Hence, multiplication by cCc_{C} really is injective on ℳ⁡(F)\mathcal{M}(F).

The map ρG\rho_{G} is surjective by the definition of 𝒫⁡(G)\mathcal{P}(G). Each matching NN of FF satisfies

ρG​(cC​uN)=pN​∑e∈Cϵe​pe=0.\rho_{G}(c_{C}u_{N})=p_{N}\sum_{e\in C}\epsilon_{e}p_{e}=0.

Thus it remains only to prove exactness in the middle.

Choose an orientation of the edges and define a polynomial ring

S:=𝐤[ye:e∈E(G)].S:=\mathbf{k}[y_{e}:e\in E(G)].

Consider the graded 𝐤\mathbf{k}-algebra homomorphism

φ:S⟶𝐤[xv:v∈V(G)],ye⟼pe(that is, yi​j⟼xi−xj).\varphi:S\longrightarrow\mathbf{k}[x_{v}:v\in V(G)],\qquad y_{e}\longmapsto p_{e}\qquad\left(\text{that is, }y_{ij}\longmapsto x_{i}-x_{j}\right).

The edge differences pe=xi−xjp_{e}=x_{i}-x_{j} of a connected graph GG span a vector space of dimension |V⁡(G)|−1|V(G)|-1. Since GG is unicyclic, |E⁡(G)|=|V⁡(G)||E(G)|=|V(G)|, so the space of linear dependences among the differences pe=xi−xjp_{e}=x_{i}-x_{j}, for e=(i,j)∈E⁡(G)e=(i,j)\in E(G), is one-dimensional. The cycle relation ∑e∈Cϵe​pe=0\sum_{e\in C}\epsilon_{e}p_{e}=0 is a nonzero such dependence, and consequently spans all of them. That is, the kernel of the degree-one part of φ\varphi is spanned by

ℓ:=∑e∈Cϵe​ye.\ell:=\sum_{e\in C}\epsilon_{e}y_{e}.

It follows that

(19) ker⁡φ=(ℓ).\ker\varphi=(\ell).

Indeed, extend ℓ\ell to a basis of S1S_{1}; the images of the remaining basis vectors are linearly independent, so S/(ℓ)S/(\ell) is the polynomial ring on those images.

For each k≥0k\geq 0, define a 𝐤\mathbf{k}-vector subspace UkU_{k} of SS by

Uk:=span𝐤⁡{yM:M∈Matchk⁡(G)}, where ​yM:=∏e∈Mye,U_{k}:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf{k}}\{y_{M}:M\in\operatorname{Match}_{k}(G)\},\qquad\text{ where }y_{M}:=\prod_{e\in M}y_{e},

and put U:=⨁k≥0UkU:=\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}U_{k}. The basis-preserving identification uM↔yMu_{M}\leftrightarrow y_{M} identifies ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) with UU as graded vector spaces, and under this identification ρG\rho_{G} is the restriction of φ\varphi to UU, while the element cCc_{C} of ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) corresponds to the element ℓ\ell of UU. Thus exactness in the middle of (18) is equivalent to

(20) U∩(ℓ)=ℓ​U​(F),U\cap(\ell)=\ell\,U(F),

where

U⁡(F):=span𝐤⁡{yN:N​ is a matching of ​F}.U(F):=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf{k}}\{y_{N}:N\text{ is a matching of }F\}.

The inclusion ℓ​U​(F)⊆U∩(ℓ)\ell U(F)\subseteq U\cap(\ell) is immediate. For the reverse inclusion, take a homogeneous element

f=ℓ​q∈U.f=\ell q\in U.

Every monomial occurring in ff is a matching monomial (i.e., a monomial of the form yMy_{M} for a matching MM of GG), hence is squarefree. Fix e∈Ce\in C. Since the coefficient of yey_{e} in ℓ\ell is nonzero and SS is a domain,

degye⁡(ℓ​q)=degye⁡q+1(q≠0).\deg_{y_{e}}(\ell q)=\deg_{y_{e}}q+1\qquad(q\neq 0).

As degye⁡f≤1\deg_{y_{e}}f\leq 1 (because every monomial occurring in ff is squarefree), we thus obtain degye⁡q=0\deg_{y_{e}}q=0. Doing this for every e∈Ce\in C shows that qq involves no cycle variables (i.e., variables of the form yey_{e} with e∈Ce\in C).

Write

q=∑αcα​yα.q=\sum_{\alpha}c_{\alpha}y^{\alpha}.

Because the yαy^{\alpha} contain no cycle variables, the monomials ye​yαy_{e}y^{\alpha}, as (e,α)(e,\alpha) varies with e∈Ce\in C, are pairwise distinct. Hence there is no cancellation in

ℓ​q=∑e∈C∑αϵe​cα​ye​yα.\ell q=\sum_{e\in C}\sum_{\alpha}\epsilon_{e}c_{\alpha}y_{e}y^{\alpha}.

Since this polynomial lies in UU, every term with cα≠0c_{\alpha}\neq 0 must be a matching monomial. It follows that yα=yNy^{\alpha}=y_{N} for a matching NN of GG. Moreover, NN cannot meet any vertex of CC: if an edge of NN met v∈V⁡(C)v\in V(C), then choosing a cycle edge ee incident with vv would make ye​yNy_{e}y_{N} a non-matching monomial. Thus NN is a matching of F=G−V⁡(C)F=G-V(C). Therefore q∈U⁡(F)q\in U(F), proving (20) and hence the exact sequence.

Taking degree kk in (18) gives a short exact sequence

0⟶ℳ​(F)k−1⟶ℳ​(G)k⟶Pk​(G)⟶0.0\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}(F)_{k-1}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}(G)_{k}\longrightarrow P_{k}(G)\longrightarrow 0.

Therefore

dimPk​(G)=mk​(G)−mk−1​(F).\dim P_{k}(G)=m_{k}(G)-m_{k-1}(F).

Finally, summing over kk and using dim𝒟​(G)k=dimPk​(G)\dim\mathcal{D}(G)_{k}=\dim P_{k}(G) gives

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)=𝔪G​(t)−t​𝔪F​(t).∎\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)=\mathfrak{m}_{G}(t)-t\mathfrak{m}_{F}(t).\qed
Proposition 5.17 (Matching-equivalent counterexamples).
  1. (a)

    There are two graphs GG and HH with 44 vertices each such that

    mk​(G)=mk​(H)for all ​k≥0, but Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)≠Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(H),t).m_{k}(G)=m_{k}(H)\quad\text{for all }k\geq 0,\qquad\text{ but }\quad\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)\neq\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(H),t).
  2. (b)

    There are two connected graphs GG and HH with 55 vertices each such that

    mk​(G)=mk​(H)for all ​k≥0, but Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)≠Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(H),t).m_{k}(G)=m_{k}(H)\quad\text{for all }k\geq 0,\qquad\text{ but }\quad\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)\neq\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(H),t).

    Moreover, GG and HH can be chosen with the same degree sequence.

  3. (c)

    There are two 22-connected graphs GG and HH with 66 vertices each such that

    mk​(G)=mk​(H)for all ​k≥0, but Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)≠Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(H),t).m_{k}(G)=m_{k}(H)\quad\text{for all }k\geq 0,\qquad\text{ but }\quad\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)\neq\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(H),t).

    Moreover, GG and HH can be chosen with the same degree sequence.

Proof.

(a) Let

G4=K1,3,H4=K3⊔K1.G_{4}=K_{1,3},\qquad H_{4}=K_{3}\sqcup K_{1}.

Both graphs have matching numbers

(m0,m1,m2)=(1,3,0).(m_{0},m_{1},m_{2})=(1,3,0).

However, G4G_{4} is connected while H4H_{4} has two connected components, so Proposition 3.5 gives

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G4),t)=1+3​t,Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(H4),t)=1+2​t.\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G_{4}),t)=1+3t,\qquad\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(H_{4}),t)=1+2t.

(b) Let G5G_{5} be the triangle on {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\} with the path 3−4−53-4-5 attached, and let H5H_{5} be the cycle 1−2−3−4−11-2-3-4-1 with the pendant edge 1−51-5. Thus

E⁡(G5)={12,23,13,34,45},E⁡(H5)={12,23,34,14,15}.\displaystyle E(G_{5})=\{12,23,13,34,45\},\qquad E(H_{5})=\{12,23,34,14,15\}.

Both graphs are connected, both have degree sequence (3,2,2,2,1)(3,2,2,2,1), and both have matching generating polynomial

𝔪G5​(t)=𝔪H5​(t)=1+5​t+4​t2.\mathfrak{m}_{G_{5}}(t)=\mathfrak{m}_{H_{5}}(t)=1+5t+4t^{2}.

For G5G_{5}, deleting the vertices of the unique triangle leaves the edge 4545, whereas for H5H_{5}, deleting the vertices of the unique 44-cycle leaves only the isolated vertex 55. Hence Theorem 5.16 gives

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G5),t)=(1+5​t+4​t2)−t⁡(1+t)=1+4​t+3​t2,\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G_{5}),t)=(1+5t+4t^{2})-t(1+t)=1+4t+3t^{2},

while

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(H5),t)=(1+5​t+4​t2)−t=1+4​t+4​t2.\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(H_{5}),t)=(1+5t+4t^{2})-t=1+4t+4t^{2}.

Thus the two graphs have the same matching data and even the same degree sequence, but different Dunkl Hilbert series.

(c) Given a graph XX on nn vertices, let X∗X^{\ast} be its cone, obtained by adjoining one new vertex adjacent to every vertex of XX. A kk-matching of X∗X^{\ast} either avoids the new vertex, or consists of a (k−1)(k-1)-matching of XX together with an edge from the new vertex to one of the n−2​k+2n-2k+2 vertices left unmatched. Hence

(21) mk​(X∗)=mk​(X)+(n−2​k+2)​mk−1​(X).m_{k}(X^{\ast})=m_{k}(X)+(n-2k+2)m_{k-1}(X).

In particular, coning preserves equality of matching numbers.

Let G5,H5G_{5},H_{5} be the two graphs constructed in part (b), and add a universal vertex 66 to each. The resulting graphs G5∗,H5∗G_{5}^{\ast},H_{5}^{\ast} are 22-connected, have the same degree sequence (5,4,3,3,3,2)(5,4,3,3,3,2), and by (21) have matching numbers

(m0,m1,m2,m3)=(1,10,19,4).(m_{0},m_{1},m_{2},m_{3})=(1,10,19,4).

By Theorem 5.9, both have dimP1=5\dim P_{1}=5 and dimP2=9\dim P_{2}=9.

The four perfect matchings of G5∗G_{5}^{\ast} give

p12​p34​p56,p12​p36​p45,p13​p26​p45,p16​p23​p45.p_{12}p_{34}p_{56},\quad p_{12}p_{36}p_{45},\quad p_{13}p_{26}p_{45},\quad p_{16}p_{23}p_{45}.

The last three satisfy the four-vertex Garnir relation

p12​p36​p45−p13​p26​p45+p16​p23​p45=0,p_{12}p_{36}p_{45}-p_{13}p_{26}p_{45}+p_{16}p_{23}p_{45}=0,

while the first polynomial is independent of their span (for instance its x1​x3​x6x_{1}x_{3}x_{6}-coefficient is nonzero and the other three have none). Any two of the last three are independent, so dimP3​(G5∗)=3\dim P_{3}(G_{5}^{\ast})=3.

The four perfect matchings of H5∗H_{5}^{\ast} give

p12​p34​p56,p14​p23​p56,p15​p23​p46,p15​p26​p34.p_{12}p_{34}p_{56},\quad p_{14}p_{23}p_{56},\quad p_{15}p_{23}p_{46},\quad p_{15}p_{26}p_{34}.

They are independent: the monomials x1​x4​x5x_{1}x_{4}x_{5}, x1​x2​x5x_{1}x_{2}x_{5}, x1​x3​x4x_{1}x_{3}x_{4}, and x1​x2​x3x_{1}x_{2}x_{3} occur, respectively, in only one of the four displayed polynomials. Hence dimP3​(H5∗)=4\dim P_{3}(H_{5}^{\ast})=4. Therefore

Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G5∗),t)=1+5​t+9​t2+3​t3,Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(H5∗),t)=1+5​t+9​t2+4​t3.\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G_{5}^{\ast}),t)=1+5t+9t^{2}+3t^{3},\qquad\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(H_{5}^{\ast}),t)=1+5t+9t^{2}+4t^{3}.

∎

Remark 5.18 (Minimality).

The examples in parts (a), (b), and (c) of Proposition 5.17 are minimal in their respective classes: among pairs of graphs on the same number of vertices with equal matching numbers but different Dunkl Hilbert series, the smallest possible number of vertices is 44 in general, 55 for connected graphs, and 66 for 22-connected graphs.

5.7. Problems

Problem 5.19.

Describe the kernel

IG=ker(𝐤[zv:v∈V]/(∑v∈Czv:C a component)⟶𝒟(G)).I_{G}=\ker\left(\mathbf{k}[z_{v}:v\in V]/(\sum_{v\in C}z_{v}:C\text{ a component})\longrightarrow\mathcal{D}(G)\right).

It contains zv2z_{v}^{2} for every vv, but in general has additional graph-dependent relations.

Problem 5.20.

Find deletion recurrences for dimPk​(G)\dim P_{k}(G) (say, for 𝐤=ℚ\mathbf{k}=\mathbb{Q}). Since matchings depend on vertex-disjointness, vertex deletion and deletion of the closed edge neighborhood are more natural here than ordinary matroid deletion–contraction.

The results on saturation proved above leave a gap for k≥3k\geq 3:

k​-linked⟹k​-saturated⟹k​-connected.k\text{-linked}\Longrightarrow k\text{-saturated}\Longrightarrow k\text{-connected}.

That is, we have a necessary combinatorial condition and a sufficient combinatorial condition for a graph to be kk-saturated, but no condition that is both at once (except for k≤2k\leq 2).

Problem 5.21.

Is there such a condition, or is it too much to ask for?

6. Log-concavity conjectures

Throughout this section, assume that 𝐤\mathbf{k} has characteristic zero. As Remark 3.6 shows, the Hilbert function can change in positive characteristic. For a finite simple graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), write

HG​(t):=Hilb⁡(𝒟⁡(G),t)=∑k=0ν⁡(G)hk​(G)​tk,r⁡(G):=|V|−c⁡(G),H_{G}(t):=\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal{D}(G),t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\nu(G)}h_{k}(G)t^{k},\qquad r(G):=|V|-c(G),

where ν⁡(G)\nu(G) is the maximum size of a matching of GG and c⁡(G)c(G) is its number of connected components, including isolated vertices. We set hk​(G)=0h_{k}(G)=0 for k>ν⁡(G)k>\nu(G). By Theorem 3.2, we have hk​(G)=dimPk​(G)h_{k}(G)=\dim P_{k}(G) for every k≥0k\geq 0. In particular, h0​(G)=1h_{0}(G)=1, h1​(G)=r​(G)h_{1}(G)=r(G), and hk​(G)>0h_{k}(G)>0 for 0≤k≤ν⁡(G)0\leq k\leq\nu(G): a matching of size kk gives a nonzero polynomial pM∈Pk​(G)p_{M}\in P_{k}(G).

Conjecture 6.1 (Log-concavity).

For every finite simple graph GG, the Hilbert function of 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) is log-concave. That is,

hk​(G)2≥hk−1​(G)​hk+1​(G)for ​1≤k<ν⁡(G).h_{k}(G)^{2}\geq h_{k-1}(G)h_{k+1}(G)\qquad\text{for }1\leq k<\nu(G).

Since the Hilbert function has no internal zeros, this conjecture would also imply its unimodality. A stronger version uses r⁡(G)r(G), the dimension of the degree-one part, as the order of normalization.

Conjecture 6.2 (Ultra-log-concavity).

For every finite simple graph GG, the sequence

(hk​(G)(r⁡(G)k))k=0ν⁡(G)\left(\frac{h_{k}(G)}{\binom{r(G)}{k}}\right)_{k=0}^{\nu(G)}

is log-concave. Equivalently, writing r=r⁡(G)r=r(G), we have

k⁡(r−k)​hk​(G)2≥(k+1)​(r−k+1)​hk−1​(G)​hk+1​(G)for ​1≤k<ν⁡(G).k(r-k)h_{k}(G)^{2}\geq(k+1)(r-k+1)h_{k-1}(G)h_{k+1}(G)\qquad\text{for }1\leq k<\nu(G).

The parameter r⁡(G)r(G) has an algebraic explanation. Omitting one vertex from each connected component leaves r⁡(G)r(G) Dunkl elements that still generate 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G), and each of these elements has square zero by (1). Thus 𝒟⁡(G)\mathcal{D}(G) is a graded quotient of

𝐤⁡[z1,…,zr]/(z12,…,zr2).\mathbf{k}[z_{1},\ldots,z_{r}]/(z_{1}^{2},\ldots,z_{r}^{2}).

In particular, hk​(G)≤(rk)h_{k}(G)\leq\binom{r}{k}. In fact, passing to a monomial initial ideal and counting inclusions between its squarefree standard monomials gives

(k+1)​hk+1​(G)≤(r−k)​hk​(G)for ​0≤k<r.(k+1)h_{k+1}(G)\leq(r-k)h_{k}(G)\qquad\text{for }0\leq k<r.

Hence the normalized sequence in Conjecture 6.2 is already nonincreasing; the conjecture asks for its log-concavity as well.

The choice of normalization matters. By Theorem 4.1,

HK5​(t)=1+4​t+5​t2.H_{K_{5}}(t)=1+4t+5t^{2}.

Normalizing its coefficients by (ν⁡(K5)k)=(2k)\binom{\nu(K_{5})}{k}=\binom{2}{k} gives (1,2,5)(1,2,5), which is not log-concave, whereas normalization by (r⁡(K5)k)=(4k)\binom{r(K_{5})}{k}=\binom{4}{k} gives (1,1,5/6)(1,1,5/6). The same example also rules out real-rootedness of HG​(t)H_{G}(t) in general. Exact rational rank computations verify Conjectures 6.1 and 6.2 for all simple graphs on at most seven vertices, up to isomorphism.

There is also a representation-theoretic strengthening of Conjecture 6.1. The group Γ=Aut⁡(G)\Gamma=\operatorname{Aut}(G) acts on 𝐤[xv:v∈V]\mathbf{k}[x_{v}:v\in V] by σ⁡(xv)=xσ⁡(v)\sigma(x_{v})=x_{\sigma(v)}. This action preserves Pk​(G)P_{k}(G): it sends each matching product pMp_{M} to ±pσ⁡(M)\pm p_{\sigma(M)}. All tensor products below are over 𝐤\mathbf{k}, with the diagonal group action.

Conjecture 6.3 (Strong equivariant log-concavity).

For every finite simple graph GG and all integers 1≤i≤j<ν⁡(G)1\leq i\leq j<\nu(G), there exists an Aut⁡(G)\operatorname{Aut}(G)-equivariant injection

Pi−1​(G)⊗Pj+1​(G)⸦⟶Pi​(G)⊗Pj​(G).P_{i-1}(G)\otimes P_{j+1}(G)\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow P_{i}(G)\otimes P_{j}(G).

Taking dimensions and setting i=ji=j recovers Conjecture 6.1. Li’s theorem [19] proves the analogous statement for the permutation representations on matchings. It does not immediately imply the conjecture above: the matching products have orientation signs under graph automorphisms and can satisfy linear relations, and an injection before passing to a quotient need not descend to an injection afterwards.

For G=KnG=K_{n}, Theorem 4.1 identifies the conjectured injection with an SnS_{n}-equivariant injection

S(n−i+1,i−1)⊗S(n−j−1,j+1)⸦⟶S(n−i,i)⊗S(n−j,j)(1≤i≤j<⌊n2⌋).S^{(n-i+1,i-1)}\otimes S^{(n-j-1,j+1)}\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow S^{(n-i,i)}\otimes S^{(n-j,j)}\qquad\left(1\leq i\leq j<\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor\right).

Here a zero second part is omitted. Equivalently, the symmetric function

s(n−i,i)∗s(n−j,j)−s(n−i+1,i−1)∗s(n−j−1,j+1)s_{(n-i,i)}*s_{(n-j,j)}-s_{(n-i+1,i-1)}*s_{(n-j-1,j+1)}

should be Schur-positive, with ∗* denoting the Kronecker (internal) product. For fixed i,ji,j, this specialization holds for all sufficiently large nn, by Gui’s inequalities for reduced Kronecker coefficients indexed by one-row partitions [14, Theorem 5.4]. The conjecture asks for every admissible nn.

Appendix A Cut quotients and zonotopal algebras: a comparison

In this section, we leave the matching algebra ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) behind and consider some other quotients of 𝐤[ue:e∈E]\mathbf{k}[u_{e}:e\in E]. We shall define analogues of the Dunkl matching subalgebra in these quotients, and state their Hilbert series. Almost all the work here has been done in [24] (sometimes implicitly), so we keep our proofs short.

Assume that the field 𝐤\mathbf{k} has characteristic 00. We shall work in the square-zero edge algebra

Φ^G:=𝐤[ue:e∈E]/(ue2:e∈E),\widehat{\Phi}_{G}:=\mathbf{k}[u_{e}:e\in E]/(u_{e}^{2}:e\in E),

which is larger than ℳ⁡(G)\mathcal{M}(G) because it only quotients out squares of edges but leaves products of distinct incident edges intact. We define the same signed incidence sums θv\theta_{v} as before, but now inside this algebra. They generate a subalgebra

𝒞Gex:=𝐤[θv:v∈V]⊆Φ^G,\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{ex}}:=\mathbf{k}[\theta_{v}:v\in V]\subseteq\widehat{\Phi}_{G},

which is known as the external graphical zonotopal algebra (the forest version of the Postnikov–Shapiro algebra); see [24, §11], as well as the zonotopal framework in [1, 15].

We shall next see what happens when we impose further monomial relations coming from edge cuts. For a nonempty proper subset S⊂VS\subset V, let

δ⁡(S):={e∈E:|e∩S|=1},dS:=|δ⁡(S)|,ηS:=∏e∈δ⁡(S)ue.\delta(S):=\{e\in E:|e\cap S|=1\},\qquad d_{S}:=|\delta(S)|,\qquad\eta_{S}:=\prod_{e\in\delta(S)}u_{e}.

Because edges internal to SS cancel in the incidence sum, we have

(22) ΘS:=∑v∈Sθv=∑e∈δ⁡(S)εS,e​ue,εS,e∈{±1}.\Theta_{S}:=\sum_{v\in S}\theta_{v}=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}\varepsilon_{S,e}u_{e},\qquad\varepsilon_{S,e}\in\{\pm 1\}.

Since the ueu_{e} are square-zero, the only surviving terms in the dSd_{S}th power ΘSdS\Theta_{S}^{d_{S}} use every cut edge e∈δ⁡(S)e\in\delta(S) exactly once. Therefore

(23) ΘSdS=dS!​(∏e∈δ⁡(S)εS,e)​ηS=±dS!​ηS.\Theta_{S}^{d_{S}}=d_{S}!\left(\prod_{e\in\delta(S)}\varepsilon_{S,e}\right)\eta_{S}=\pm d_{S}!\,\eta_{S}.

In characteristic zero this shows, in particular, that every cut monomial ηS\eta_{S} already belongs to 𝒞Gex\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{ex}}.

The relation with the usual external and central power ideals makes the next quotient transparent. Put

RV:=𝐤[zv:v∈V]/(∑v∈Vzv),ℓS:=∑v∈Szv.R_{V}:=\mathbf{k}[z_{v}:v\in V]/\left(\sum_{v\in V}z_{v}\right),\qquad\ell_{S}:=\sum_{v\in S}z_{v}.

The standard graphical power-ideal presentations ([24, Theorem 11.1 and Corollary 10.5]) are

(24) 𝒞Gex\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{ex}} ≅RV/(ℓSdS+1:∅≠S⊊V),\displaystyle\cong R_{V}/(\ell_{S}^{d_{S}+1}:\varnothing\neq S\subsetneq V),
(25) 𝒞Gcentral\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{central}} ≅RV/(ℓSdS:∅≠S⊊V).\displaystyle\cong R_{V}/(\ell_{S}^{d_{S}}:\varnothing\neq S\subsetneq V).

Here zvz_{v} maps to θv\theta_{v}. These presentations are the graphical cases of the external and central zonotopal algebras; see [24, Secs. 9 and 11] and [1, 15].

Proposition A.1 (The cut quotient inside the incidence-sum algebra).

For a connected graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) in characteristic zero,

𝒞Gex/(ηS:∅≠S⊊V)≅𝒞Gcentral.\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{ex}}/(\eta_{S}:\varnothing\neq S\subsetneq V)\cong\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{central}}.

Consequently, if m=|E|m=|E| and r=|V|−1r=|V|-1, then

Hilb⁡(𝒞Gex/(ηS),t)=Hilb⁡(𝒞Gcentral,t)=tm−r​TG​(1,t−1),\operatorname{Hilb}\left(\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{ex}}/(\eta_{S}),t\right)=\operatorname{Hilb}\left(\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{central}},t\right)=t^{m-r}T_{G}(1,t^{-1}),

where TGT_{G} denotes the Tutte polynomial of GG (see, e.g., [12]).

Proof.

Under the presentation (24), the element ℓSdS\ell_{S}^{d_{S}} maps, by (23), to a nonzero scalar multiple of ηS\eta_{S}. Thus quotienting 𝒞Gex\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{ex}} by all ηS\eta_{S} adds exactly the relations ℓSdS=0\ell_{S}^{d_{S}}=0. The resulting presentation is (25). The Hilbert-series formula is the standard central zonotopal specialization of the Tutte polynomial [1, 15]; e.g., combine [24, Theorem 3.3 or Theorem 9.1] with [12, Theorem 3.12]. ∎

There is a second quotient by the same cut monomials ηS\eta_{S}, obtained by imposing them on the whole square-zero edge algebra rather than only on its incidence-sum subalgebra. This is larger, and it has an elementary basis. Let

Icut:=(ηS:∅≠S⊊V)⊆Φ^G.I_{\mathrm{cut}}:=(\eta_{S}:\varnothing\neq S\subsetneq V)\subseteq\widehat{\Phi}_{G}.

For F⊆EF\subseteq E, write uF:=∏e∈Fueu_{F}:=\prod_{e\in F}u_{e}.

Proposition A.2 (The ambient cut quotient).

For connected GG, the set

{uF:G∖F​ is connected}\{u_{F}:G\setminus F\text{ is connected}\}

is a basis of Φ^G/Icut\widehat{\Phi}_{G}/I_{\mathrm{cut}}. Hence

Hilb⁡(Φ^G/Icut,t)\displaystyle\operatorname{Hilb}(\widehat{\Phi}_{G}/I_{\mathrm{cut}},t) =∑H⊆G;H​ connected spanningtm−|H|\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}H\subseteq G;\\ H\text{ connected spanning}\end{subarray}}t^{m-|H|}
=tm−r​TG​(1,1+t−1).\displaystyle=t^{m-r}T_{G}(1,1+t^{-1}).
Proof.

The squarefree monomials uFu_{F} form a basis of Φ^G\widehat{\Phi}_{G}, and IcutI_{\mathrm{cut}} is a monomial ideal. Thus uFu_{F} survives in the quotient exactly when it is not divisible by any ηS\eta_{S}, that is, exactly when δ⁡(S)⊈F\delta(S)\nsubseteq F for every nonempty proper S⊂VS\subset V. But a deletion set FF contains a whole cut δ⁡(S)\delta(S) if and only if G∖FG\setminus F has no edge from SS to V∖SV\setminus S, equivalently if and only if G∖FG\setminus F is disconnected. This proves the basis statement and the first Hilbert-series formula.

For the second formula, use the corank–nullity expansion

TG​(1,y)=∑H⊆G;H​ connected spanning(y−1)|H|−rT_{G}(1,y)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}H\subseteq G;\\ H\text{ connected spanning}\end{subarray}}(y-1)^{|H|-r}

(see, e.g., [12, Proposition 3.10]) and substitute y=1+t−1y=1+t^{-1}. ∎

Thus the same cut relations produce two different but closely related objects. They fit into the diagram

𝒞Gex⊆Φ^G↓↓𝒞Gcentral⊆Φ^G/Icut\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{ccc}\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{ex}}&\subseteq&\widehat{\Phi}_{G}\\[5.69054pt] \downarrow&&\downarrow\\[5.69054pt] \mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{central}}&\subseteq&\widehat{\Phi}_{G}/I_{\mathrm{cut}}\end{array}

(whose bottom row is injective because of [24, Corollary 10.5]33 3 Indeed, the algebra ℬG\mathcal{B}_{G} in [24] is our 𝒞Gcentral\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{central}}, while the algebra ΦG\Phi_{G} in [24] is our Φ^G/Icut\widehat{\Phi}_{G}/I_{\mathrm{cut}}. Thus, by identifying ℬG\mathcal{B}_{G} with the subalgebra 𝒞G\mathcal{C}_{G} of ΦG\Phi_{G}, [24, Corollary 10.5] shows that 𝒞Gcentral\mathcal{C}_{G}^{\mathrm{central}} embeds into ΦG=Φ^G/Icut\Phi_{G}=\widehat{\Phi}_{G}/I_{\mathrm{cut}}.). The lower-left algebra has total dimension TG​(1,1)T_{G}(1,1), the number of spanning trees (by Proposition A.1). The lower-right algebra has total dimension TG​(1,2)T_{G}(1,2), the number of connected spanning subgraphs (by Proposition A.2); its grading records the number of deleted edges. More precisely, if

RG​(p)=∑H⊆G;H​ connected spanningp|H|​(1−p)m−|H|R_{G}(p)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}H\subseteq G;\\ H\text{ connected spanning}\end{subarray}}p^{|H|}(1-p)^{m-|H|}

is the all-terminal reliability polynomial, then

Hilb⁡(Φ^G/Icut,t)=(1+t)m​RG​((1+t)−1).\operatorname{Hilb}(\widehat{\Phi}_{G}/I_{\mathrm{cut}},t)=(1+t)^{m}R_{G}((1+t)^{-1}).
